Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that on June 3 I announced to the house that the government had decided to recommend to parliament that capital assistance be provided in the form of a subsidy of $25,000 per mile for the construction of the Lake Cache-St. Felicien section of the branch line from Beattyville to St. Felicien previously authorized by parliament. Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a reply to these four questions. Question No. 4 calls for an oral answer, and I am going to answer all four orally.
With regard to these four questions, public policy, as indicated by statutory provisions and otherwise, requires that all information

Questions
and sources of information respecting revenue matters be treated as secret. Consequently no answer can be given to a question which might tend to disclose a source of information.

May I say that throughout our 27 offices in Canada we have photostatic equipment to make photostatic copies of documents and also, in some of the offices, to make microfilm copies of these documents. The purpose of this is that, in the event of books and records being seized from a taxpayer, by having copies of the documents, the original ones may be more quickly returned to the taxpayer.
It then asks, "For what purpose or purposes were such photostatic copies made?" The purposes are that they may be used, if necessary, in the event of prosecution, whether that be in the civil court or used in the case of an appeal and whether that appeal be before the income tax appeal board or the exchequer court. With regard to the question, "In how many cases were such photostatic copies brought to the attention of the minister?" subtopic: SUGGESTED POLICY FOR STABILIZATION OF INDUSTRY
SUGGESTED POLICY FOR STABILIZATION OF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because we in this group believe

that at this session of parliament the government has refused to admit the serious situation which has developed in our agricultural industry, and as a result of that refusal has failed to implement measures in our agricultural policy which would stabilize this most important industry, we take advantage of this opportunity to bring this grievance to the attention of the house at this time. The agricultural producer is the only producer in this country who has no control over his costs of production or the prices he receives for his product. We feel that we must have implemented in our agricultural policies some measures which will bring about greater stability to the industry.
Our agricultural industry is trying to survive in an economy which arbitrarily administers both costs and prices. We maintain that if agriculture is going to have returned to it its fair share of the national income, that can be done only if there is some system of parity prices or as an alternative some other measure of control over the cost of production. When we realize that the agricultural producer receives only 8-7 per cent of the national income, when we realize that 20 per cent of the people of Canada are actively engaged in industry, then we have reason to become seriously alarmed at the situation.
We in the C.C.F. believe that this question of a fair relationship between the cost of production and the price received for the commodity produced is soon going to become the greatest single problem which will have to be coped with by farm organizations in this country. We submit that all the talk we hear about the inefficiency of the agricultural producer, and that because of that inefficiency he cannot expect to get his fair share of the national income, is false. I think we should look at what the records show in regard to this question of inefficiency.
We find that in 1951 we had in Canada
60,000	fewer farms than there were in 1941. I do not mean by that that 60,000 farms have been taken out of production; they have merely been absorbed, in order to provide more efficient and economical units in the industry. Another significant fact is that there are 53,000 fewer farmers now engaged in agriculture than was the case in 1941. In other words, in the period 1941 to 1951 there has been no reduction in the cultivated acreage in this country; we have been able to maintain our production in spite of the fact that the industry has lost some 53,000 farmers. In 1941 agricultural production in this country was represented by the figure 109 whereas in 1951, despite the loss to the industry of some 53,000 workers, that production is represented by the figure 155. That
Agriculture
is according to the figures in the Canada Year Book. This industry has produced 50 per cent more during that period with a considerable loss in manpower and therefore the argument that the farmer is inefficient, that he must become more efficient in order to participate in a fair share of the national income, is an allegation which has absolutely no truth in it.
That is one of the facts which I think we should not overlook. As a matter of fact, the history of those years proves that as our efficiency increased our share of the national income steadily declined. The question I should like to ask is what has happened to the cash that must have accrued because of this increased efficiency. I suggest without hesitation that it was high-jacked by those people who at the present time have tremendous control over the farmer's cost of production. Therefore I submit that it is a poor argument to say that our receiving a fair share of the national income is contingent on our ability to produce efficiently.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort asks the government to consider the establishment of a system of parity prices for agricultural products. The meaning of 
parity prices is that the price of farm products shall be related to the farmer's cost of production and those things that the farmer must buy. Every other industry in this country, every other group in this country, has already achieved a system of parity prices in its own particular field. By that I mean that any industry apart from agriculture, in setting the price for its finished product, obtains the cost of production plus a return in addition to the cost of production. If the cost of production goes up, then certainly those other industries will increase their prices.
If we are going to establish a system of parity prices for farm prices, then I think it is extremely important that the government do everything possible, not only to obtain the best possible prices for our agricultural products on the export markets, but to expand our export markets so that we may have full agricultural production at home. I was pleased indeed with the Prime Minister's answer to my question as to whether the government was exploring the possibility of selling Canadian wheat and barley to China. I take it from his answer that if the Chinese government produces the cash at the regular selling price, sales will be made. The Prime Minister went on to say that China, in obtaining food supplies, has ordinarily entered into barter arrangements and that Canada was not adopting such a policy. I believe this government should explore the possibility of making barter arrangements for the sale of Canadian wheat.
As a matter of fact, I think the government should do far more than explore the possibility. The government should secure wheat markets wherever they exist, if they can be secured by signing barter deals on a reasonable basis. I for one-and I believe the wheat producers in western Canada also -would be pleased if barter arrangements could be made with any country in the world at fair terms in order to sell our wheat and coarse grains. Some may suggest that there would be something wrong with entering into a barter arrangement with China for the exchange of Canadian wheat; but I think it would be much better for China and Canada to exchange goods than to exchange bombs. I believe that an increase in trade amongst all countries of the world is an essential to peace, and the growing indications that world trade is once again expanding are a good omen for the future.
We in this group for some months now have been pointing out to the government that, by its policy, which is cash on the line, and by not allowing any different policy, we are losing and have lost a great many

important wheat markets to Canada. The United States day by day is continuing to expand its share of the world market for wheat, and it is expanding in precisely the same way as the C.C.F. over the years has asked our government to consider in suggesting policies that our government should follow. We believe that if countries like India and Pakistan wish to accept wheat in return for local currencies, our government should not hesitate to accept such currencies which at some future date we shall be able to use in order to purchase goods from those countries that subsequently will be used by the Canadian nation.
In this group we do not believe that there is anything wrong with gifts of wheat under certain circumstances. If any country of the world experiences famine conditions and is short of cash, under those circumstances we believe that the Canadian government should consider a gift of Canadian wheat. We do not think the farmers should be asked to give the wheat but rather we think that the nation as a whole should give the wheat, under those circumstances, as a part of national policy. In this way I think we would be making a further contribution to peace. We have already given some wheat away in the past under the Colombo plan, but the $26 million voted for the Colombo plan is an insignificant amount as related to this great problem of feeding hungry people.
Through accepting local currencies the United States government is succeeding in selling greater quantities of United States wheat, even though all of us know that United States wheat is inferior in every respect. The results of that action by the United States are clear and are set out in the latest Wheat Review for May, 1955, in which it is shown that in the August to April period of this year United States exports were 204 million bushels, an increase of 58 million bushels from the figures in the comparable period a year previously.
What is Canada's position? Our exports in the same period this year were 189-4 million bushels, an increase of only 1 [DOT] 6 million bushels. There is there a clear indication that United States policies are functioning in that they have been successful in getting rid of additional quantities of United States wheat on the export market.
When we have advanced these policies the government has said no, and we have seen slip away many foreign markets for Canadian wheat in the western world until today, if Canada is to increase its share in the world wheat market, she must sell to such countries as Poland and Hungary because the United States and the Argentine have
Agriculture
together increased their sales to western countries. We have no objection whatsoever to the sale of wheat to Poland or to Hungary. We welcome sales of wheat to any country in the world. However, we say that the government months ago could have increased sales of wheat to countries in the western world if it had followed the suggestions put forward by the C.C.F. group, and that we would not now be obliged to rely on sales to communist countries as apparently the only remaining method by which Canadian sales of wheat can be increased.
We are not only losing the markets for wheat to United States but we have lost substantial markets to the Argentine. The chairman of the wheat board, speaking before the agriculture committee a few weeks ago, told us that the Argentine, through a barter deal, had captured a large part of the market in Brazil and the market in Chile. The Argentine share of the world wheat market in the period to which I have referred was 102-6 million bushels, an increase of 16 million bushels from the figures for a similar period the year before.
In these barter arrangements undertaken by the Argentine and in the United States sales policy for wheat, do the wheat producers suffer? The answer is no. The Canadian initial price or floor price for wheat is $1.40. The United States floor price for wheat in the same period is $2.24 a bushel and the Argentine floor price is $2.72 a bushel. In other words, the United States government and the government of the Argentine have been successful in expanding their share of the world wheat market and at the same time have paid a much higher price to their wheat producers than that which has been paid in Canada.
As a matter of fact, Canada has the dubious distinction of having the lowest guaranteed price for wheat of any country anywhere in the world. I hold in my hand the Alberta wheat pool budget of July 1, 1955, and it lists the wheat prices in some 30 countries of the world. Canada is at the bottom of the list, with the lowest price, namely $1.40 a bushel. Is our government going to say that the Canadian economy is such that we cannot pay our wheat farmers more than $1.40 a bushel or as much as such countries as India, Iran, Ireland, Italy, Japan? I could go on and name all of these countries. The low price starts with Canada at $1.40 and goes up to Norway with a price of $3.43 a bushel; Finland with $3.95 a bushel; and Chile at the top with a guaranteed floor price of $4.50 a bushel. The treatment that Canadian wheat producers are handed out under the present policy is nothing less than shameful.

Agriculture
The motion we have before the house this morning is one that asks for parity prices for all agricultural products. We believe that the establishment of adequate floor prices for farm products is not only something that is essential to agriculture but is something that is in the interests of the whole Canadian nation. I am hopeful that this amendment will commend itself to hon. members of the house and that it will receive wide support when the vote is taken.

Mr. Speaker, I may say that we in the Social Credit group intend to support the amendment. I might point out that on former occasions we have outlined what we consider to be the essentials of a sound agriculture policy. They are, first of all, that the support prices for agricultural products should be on the basis of a two-price system; second, that steps must be taken to extend the market for agricultural products, both internally and externally; and third, the need for a sound crop insurance policy.
On former occasions, I have stressed the fact that the government would have every justification for maintaining adequate support prices; and the justification for that, of course, goes back to the years during the war when ceilings were maintained on agricultural prices and when the prime minister of the day promised that that was part of the stabilization program and that, in return, the farmers would be guaranteed stabilized prices after the war. As a sign of good faith, the government introduced the Agricultural Prices Support Act. The only trouble is that there is always a great deal of uncertainty about what the support price will be under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. Although the minister has announced a formula under which the support price will be set,-that is, he used the base years of 1943, 1944 and 1945-if he would give assurance that the prices of all the main farm products would be supported on the basis of those three base years at 100 per cent of prices during that period, 1 do not think that agriculture would have any ground for complaint. Unfortunately, however, the minister, who at one time apparently did seem to adhere to that principle, has now found it very convenient to use the suggestion of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, namely that prices of agricultural products should only be supported at 65 to 85 per cent of parity. I claim there is every justification for maintaining prices in Canada of agricultural products at 100 per cent of parity on the basis of the years 1943, 1944 and 1945 for the very simple reason that the prices of agricultural products during those years (Mr. Argue.]
could not under any consideration be considered high in relation to the prices of other commodities. During those years the prices of agricultural products were controlled, and therefore the prices of farm products in those years could not be considered high in relation to the prices of other commodities. Therefore why should prices of farm products not be maintained today in a similar relationship to the prices of other commodities as existed in those three years?
We in this group absolutely oppose the principle put forward by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture that farm support prices should only be maintained at 65 to 85 per cent of parity. We support wholeheartedly the proposals of the interprovincial farmers' union for a two-price system. The minister has pointed out that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture stretches right across Canada and therefore is an organization that should be given more consideration than the farmers' union, which is a western organization. But let the minister not forget that the farmers' union also includes Ontario and the farmers' union represents bona fide members. Every member of the farmers' union is a paying member of that organization, a man who has joined the organization because he believes in it. That is not true of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I doubt if there are half a dozen farmers in my whole constituency who are actually members of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture as a result of having paid a fee. They are members indirectly because they are members of the wheat pool or some other organization but they are not paid-up members in the same way that the members of the farmers' union are.
I consider the farmers' union represents to a far greater degree the aims, objectives and wishes of farmers in western Canada than does the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. The inter provincial farmers' union has advocated a two-price system, and we support a two-price system 100 per cent. I am glad to see that the government has supported in part the idea of the two-price system because we have butter supported at a parity price and we have butter sold abroad at the world market price. In other words, the government itself has already adopted in part the principle of a two-price system. I hope the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) will note that because when he spoke he bitterly attacked the idea of selling any of our farm products abroad for a lower price than we sold them internally.
Now the government is doing it and I say they are fully justified in doing it. I will deal with that later at some length.

Under a two-price system, prices of farm products consumed in Canada shall be maintained at 100 per cent of parity on the basis of the three past years used by the minister, 1943, 1944 and 1945, and prices of goods exported abroad shall be set at the best price obtainable supported by reasonable support prices where necessary.
It is interesting to note that the secondary industries have been operating on that principle for years. They set their internal price at a level that they consider will return them a fair profit and sell their surpluses abroad for the best price they are able to obtain. Time and again I have priced in England farm machinery manufactured in Canada and have found that such machinery was being sold cheaper in England than it was being sold in Canada, showing that they were operating under a two-price system. But in agriculture that has never been the system. In agriculture the small surplus that we export abroad has invariably set the price for the larger percentage consumed in Canada.
Let us take beef. In 1954 we only exported abroad 5-6 per cent of our total production of beef. The rest was consumed in Canada. If you take all agricultural products with the exception of wheat you will find that approximately 94 per cent of all foods produced in Canada are consumed in this country. Why should we let the 6 per cent exported abroad set the price for the 94 per cent consumed in Canada? Of course the minister will say we do not do that altogether because under the Agricultural Prices Support Act we have support prices. But let me point out to the minister that support prices under that act are not as high as they should be, using the formula of the minister. Eggs today have a support price of 38 cents, or only 56 per cent of parity on the basis of 1943, 1944 and 1945.

speechtext:
I have not been selling eggs lately, but I do not doubt for one minute that if I had shipped 30 dozen crates of eggs I would be lucky in the past few years to get 38 cents a dozen for them at the peak of production. With respect to butter, the support price is 58 cents, or only 84.6 per cent of parity. I obtained these figures from the agricultural prices support board. The minister did not like it when I quoted figures from the bureau of statistics so I wrote the agricultural prices support board and got figures from them. With respect to hogs, the support price is 23 cents, which is only 83 per cent of parity. In view of the fact that the minister is using the three years, 1943, 1944 and 1945, I think the farmers have a right to expect the support prices to be maintained at 100 per cent under that formula. I know the minister will try to get out the back door by saying that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has suggested 65 per cent to 85 per cent of parity. I think the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has done the farmers of this country a great disservice in making that suggestion in view of the fact that the farmers were guaranteed, in return for the sacrifices they made during the war, that prices would be stabilized after the war at a fair relationship.
Then there is the question of wheat. We are not on the agricultural estimates so I suppose it is all right to discuss wheat on this general motion. I pointed out some time ago that under a two-price system the support price of wheat today would be approximately $1.81 a bushel. According to the bureau of statistics the parity price for wheat would be $2.27 a bushel. About 20 per cent of our wheat, we will say, is consumed in Canada and the other 80 per cent is exported abroad. If the other 80 per cent were sold at the average between the high and the low of the international wheat agreement that would result in an average on total sales of $1.81 a bushel.
I mentioned that some months ago, and it is very interesting to note that since that time the United States has announced their support price for wheat and set it at $1.81 a bushel, so we would then have our support price for wheat on exactly the same level as that of the United States. Of course the support price

.	Agriculture
of $1.81 in the United States is being paid on the understanding that the farmers will reduce their acreage, but there is no reason why we should do the same thing in Canada because we have not had an increase in acreage in our country in the last few years, as they have had in the United States. The United States brought about a tremendous expansion in acreage and they are really getting back to the level of their former acreage. Therefore there would be no reason why Canada should reduce its acreage.
We come now to the important question of surpluses. I mentioned at the start that one of the most necessary things to do in order to get a fair deal for agriculture is to find markets for our produce both internally and externally. The problem of surpluses is one that has been giving the great producing nations of the world a good deal of concern. We have had from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and even the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) at times statements which would almost give the impression that there is no very great want in the world. Perhaps it is not fair to say that in regard to the Minister of Agriculture, although he did mention that in India he knew of 100 million people who were better off than the people in Canada, which would tend to give people a different idea of conditions in India from what most of us have. If anybody has any doubt about what the world situation is, he should read a statement made by Mr. Gove Hambidge, the representative of the FAO for North America. I should like to quote what he said when he presented a brief before the Senate earlier this year:
Over against this prosperous group of countries blessed with plenty of food and so many of the good things of life, you have another group still far down the scale of economic and physical wellbeing. They include half the people of the world or more, and they are still poor and undernourished, many of them living in bleak hovels, without enough clothing, illiterate and uneducated, dying young, lacking the modern tools and equipment necessary for good production, and often without enough physical vigour to do what we would call a really good day's work even though they work as hard as they can. But better living and greater abundance are possible for these great masses of mankind, and they are becoming more and more sharply aware that their lives and the lives of their children can be better.
It is this possibility of better times, opened up by modern scientific developments but not yet reaching down to all the levels of mankind, that creates much of the tension among nations and within nations today. When people see something they want very badly and think they can have it and are entitled to it, they are likely to try to get it by violent means if more peaceful ones do not seem to work. And there are plenty of troublemakers around to encourage them to use violence.
So the first fundamental need, as I see it, is the necessary effort to bring about a much better balance in the world than we now have.

In the light of that statement, I do not think anyone would seriously challenge the argument that there is great hunger in many parts of the world today. Just as long as that hunger exists, no nation can be justified in reducing its production. As Mr. Hambidge points out, when the masses of people in certain nations are hungry and see other countries reducing their production, then it is bound to cause a lot of friction and discontent in those nations. That, in itself, would do more to breed communism, I believe, than any other one thing, and would in the minds of those people justify the claim of the reds that capitalism has failed when it is not able to distribute surplus goods to hungry people and the only policy of those nations is to reduce their production.
I was somewhat amused by a statement that was made by a man who should have known better but apparently allowed politics to distort his mind on this subject. I have a statement that was made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), as reported in the Edmonton Journal. Speaking at Viking on June 17, he had this to say:
I've heard Social Crediters say we should reduce our stocks of wheat by accepting foreign currencies or even by giving them away.
This has an appeal when we see our wheat piling up whilst others starve, but in Ottawa we have an obligation to keep trade on solid ground. If we started bartering or giving away, we would disturb international markets and in the long run we would injure not only ourselves but also those we seek to help.
We should try to keep trade on a multilateral,
economic basis and disregard emotional superficial solutions to our problems.
It is interesting to note that the minister calls the acceptance of foreign currency and barter a superficial emotional appeal. I wonder if the minister of external affairs would call the recommendations of the food and agriculture organization, one of the ancillary organizations of the United Nations, superficial and emotional? I believe he should study the recommendations that were made by a body of experts set up by the FAO. I quote from a statement of the functions of the international commodity clearing house, as contained in IFAP bulletin, October 1949. These were a few of the recommendations:
(1)	Subject to provisions outlined below, the purchase of stocks of commodities that are in surplus in the country in which those stocks appear.
(2)	The negotiation of sales in inconvertible currencies in order to assist in maintaining the flow of trade during periods of exchange disequilibrium; such payments being guaranteed by the buying countries against losses from exchange depreciation.
(3)	The negotiation of sales at special prices below the market to countries in need, under

strictly defined conditions of use; for example, for relief purposes, special nutritional programs, or for development projects.
(4)	As a long run function, the holding of stocks acquired in periods of surplus as reserves to protect the interests of consumers in periods of shortage.
(5)	The negotiation of bilateral or multilateral trading agreements, or exchanges of commodities on a barter basis.
Now, the FAO recommended the disposal of goods in return for foreign currency and in return for barter deals. The minister of external affairs says that is a superficial emotional suggestion. I do not think he would, on the other hand, brand the FAO as a superficial organization, although, mind you, these were probably their most outstanding recommendations to date.
I want to say just a few words regarding the deal with Poland and Czechoslovakia. We in this group have absolutely no opposition to the sale of goods to nations behind the iron curtain, provided certain definite principles are recognized. First of all, we say we have an obligation to make certain that the needs of the home market are satisfied before we start making goods available to people behind the iron curtain. We should be satisfied that the people in our own country are getting enough of the commodities we are exporting to these countries. I would suggest that one very good way of disposing of butter in Canada before we start disposing of it to Czechoslovakia would be to give additional supplies of butter to all those people receiving certain social payments, such as family allowances and old age pensions.
We could adopt a program similar to that which was adopted in the United States in the thirties and provide these people with stamps, which would give them the right to obtain additional supplies of butter with every purchase of butter they make. This would help dispose of a lot of surplus butter to people who need it in Canada. It worked out satisfactorily in the United States. It helped them dispose of their surplus commodities at that time. These stamps were only issued to people who were on relief, but we could go a step further than relief and could give them to all those people receiving payments from the government by way of family allowances, old age pensions, war veterans allowances and such things as that.
Then we feel a program of course has to be adopted to expand the purchasing power of the people in Canada so as to make it possible to provide a total market for all the goods in this country and all the goods brought into this country in return for goods exported. I am not suggesting we can consume all the wheat we produce, but we can
Agriculture
consume the goods brought into this country in return for our wheat.
The next step would be to make surplus goods available, first of all, to friendly nations; to make them available not merely through the orthodox channels of trade but to make those goods available by the acceptance of foreign currencies, by barter deals and in some cases by gifts. Then, to the extent we still have surplus goods left over, we could make them available to the countries behind the iron curtain. But let us insist, when we make goods available to nations behind the iron curtain, that they must give that transaction enough publicity so the people know that these goods are coming from Canada, and not merely being made available from one of their own satellites. In the light of what I have said we intend to support the amendment.

I would point out that in raising this subject in the house by way of questions, and by way of a motion that the house adjourn to debate the subject, we were seeking information in regard to transactions which had not been explained either to the House of Commons or to the public. It was only by directing those questions to the government that we obtained the information we now have as to the terms upon which it is 
proposed to carry out the sales, if the transactions are completed. And I might point out that we are not sure even yet whether or not the transactions in fact have been completed. We had the statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that they had not been, and we had the statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that they had. We also have the statement of Mr. Swartz in Winnipeg that negotiations had been completed for these sales. There is still uncertainty as to the details of those transactions. We sought to ascertain what the financial arrangements were. So far as this transaction is concerned we made it perfectly clear, as Hansard will show, that we are not opposed to arrangements with Poland or other countries for the sale of our wheat, but we do regard it as our duty to ascertain on behalf of members of the House of Commons and the people of Canada what the financial arrangements behind those transactions are.
That has been the purpose of raising the question in the house; and we still want more information than we yet have as to the negotiations and the terms of the various arrangements.
It will be recalled by hon. members that we pointed out that reports in reliable newspapers referred not only to the sale of wheat but also the sale of other commodities. As yet we have no information with regard to these other negotiations, either as to the basic terms of the transactions, or otherwise.
The information we have obtained is that it is proposed to carry out a sale of Canadian wheat to Poland under an arrangement whereby the government of Poland would pay 15 per cent of the agreed cost of the wheat; through the Export Credits Insurance Corporation advances to the communist government in Poland would he guaranteed by Canadian banks, to the extent of 85 per cent of the cost of the wheat. Under that arrangement the Canadian taxpayer therefore becomes responsible for 85 per cent of the cost of the transaction. Whether that is a good or a bad financial arrangement, it is obvious that it is the duty of members of the house to ascertain the facts when negotiations of that kind are under consideration.
It will be recalled by every member in the house that we have been urging for several years that this government step up its activities in the marketing of our wheat to our former customers. We have emphasized the need for a more vigorous selling of our surplus wheat to the United Kingdom and to other countries in the sterling area. We have made it clear that we

support the sale of wheat or other surplus commodities under any appropriate arrangements that do not conflict with Canadian security and Canadian interests. I made it emphatically clear in this house only a few days ago that we are not raising a question in regard to these transactions upon the basis of any blanket opposition to dealing with countries beyond the iron curtain in matters of this kind. We do say that if there are to be specially favourable arrangements in regard to food products there should not be more favourable arrangements with countries beyond the iron curtain than with countries friendly to us and in fact joined with us in an effort to defend ourselves against the possibility of aggression from beyond the iron curtain. That has been the sum total of the position we have taken.
I would point out that in the transaction as it has been explained to us the Canadian taxpayers are called upon to guarantee 85 per cent of the cost of this wheat to the communist government of Poland. The arrangement calls for the repayment of that 85 per cent within one year. I think the government should make a statement to us as to its overall policy in this regard. Does it believe that at a time when we are being called upon to spend so much to defend ourselves against possible aggression from beyond the iron curtain we should accept without some adequate assurances the credit arrangements put forward by these governments which are imposing upon us the necessity for these huge expenditures?
It will be recalled that only a few days ago in this house I asked the government if it would not be desirable for it to consider the possibility of using a substantial part of our surplus wheat as further gifts under the Colombo plan to those friendly countries which are in need of wheat at this time. After all, this wheat will be paid for by the Canadian taxpayers. What we want is some explanation of the over-all policy under which these arrangements are being made. I do think that most certainly, at a time when NATO will be meeting in Paris within days to consider broad plans for the colossal preparations being made for the defence of our freedom against possible aggression by communist governments, we should have explained to us the policy of this government under which 85 per cent of the cost of these products is being assumed by the Canadian taxpayers when the products will be taken over by governments beyond the iron curtain.
I subscribe to the idea that has been put forward here that in every way possible we should seek to impress upon the minds of
Agriculture
the people in the countries beyond the iron curtain that there is no antagonism on our part toward them as human beings in need of the ordinary necessities of life. Not only do I subscribe to that statement this morning, but hon. members will recall that I put forward a proposition in this house a few days ago that we should seek every opportunity of carrying beyond the iron curtain our belief that we have common ideals and common purposes with the people who live beyond the iron curtain.
I hope that no hon. member of this house will forget that the communist governments are unlikely to explain to their people that any wheat or other products that come to them have been obtained under favourable terms from the Canadian government. I am not raising that as an argument against carrying out appropriate transactions by sound financial methods. However, I hope that no hon. member will be under the impression that these communist governments will say to their people, "You are receiving this additional wheat because of generous arrangements made by the government of Canada."
I remember an incident which occurred in Italy while I was there a few years ago and which caused a great deal of comment. As every hon. member knows, there are a great number of communist municipal councils throughout Italy. In one of the hill towns of Tuscany a great celebration was arranged by the communist council of that municipality to distribute to the people of that community wheat which they said had been _ sent to them by the government of Russia. The only flaw in the arrangement was that the bags in which the wheat was delivered had a maple leaf on them. They had come from Canada and the communist council had not noticed the maple leaf and wording in English which made it quite clear that the wheat had come from Canada under arrangements made at that time in this country. I recall other similar occasions and I know that many hon. members have read of similar cases.
I recall another instance which happened only last year while I was in Germany; this has certain amusing aspects to it but it does illustrate the way these things happen. A worker in a village in East Germany was helping to load potatoes grown in his own community into a car destined for Leipzig. Of course in East Germany as in all other communist countries you must have a passport even to move from town to town. This man had hung up his coat containing his passport and wallet inside the car in which he was loading potatoes. He turned around to

Agriculture
do something else and then discovered that the door of the car had been closed and his coat was inside.
He did his utmost to get the communist boss to open the car but that communist official was not taking any chances by doing anything of that kind. A friend of this man suggested that if he could get to Leipzig ahead of the car he might be able to get into it. He got to Leipzig, the car was opened and he recovered his wallet and passport. Naturally he was a very happy man. Then, as is the habit in Germany as well as in other countries, he went to a nearby beer hall to get a glass of beer. Whether it was after the first or second glass was not explained to me, but at some point he went on to tell of his experience. When he got into the car in Leipzig he found chalked on the car in large letters a statement that the potatoes contained therein were being delivered to the people by their friends in Russia. This man had worked loading that car in his own village in East Germany the night before and he thought this was a great joke. Unfortunately when he told the joke an MVD man was present and this unfortunate worker is now serving a two-year term for insulting the government of Russia.
That is the kind of thing that goes on. They do not take any chances of the people of those countries being impressed by the generosity of the free nations of the west. Nevertheless I am prepared to agree that by every means within our power we should attempt to break open the iron curtain. I said here in this house the other day that in common with the people beyond the iron curtain, we want to live. In every way we can, consistent with the defence of our own freedom, we are anxious to see presented to the minds of the people themselves beyond the iron curtain the fact-and the very important fact-that we have nothing but good will for them as human beings and as individuals with all of the natural hopes and aspirations of human beings on this planet. Let us not be too confident, however, that any communist government is going to proclaim to its own people the friendly acts of our government or of the people of this country; and this, of course, would be an act of the people of Canada, because it will be the Canadian taxpayers who are paying the money.
I therefore sum up these remarks simply by saying, if there are going to be transactions of this kind, let us know what the transactions are, let us be sure we are not extending more favourable terms to communist governments beyond the iron curtain than we are extending to the governments with which we are associated in the common 
defence of freedom; and, above all, let us be sure that there is a fair statement of policy as to the arrangements under which these transactions are being carried out. That is all we ask. Within those terms we are ready to see any sound transactions carried out with countries anywhere in the world.
We do, however, repeat the demands that we have made for several years that a much more vigorous effort be made to reopen those traditional markets in the United Kingdom and in other countries to which we have been selling wheat for so many years, by methods that we can employ to sell them the wheat and other foodstuffs they need, the wheat and other foodstuffs we also need to sell. This party wants a vigorous and well-understood method of disposing of our foodstuffs. We want to see the wheat moving from the farms in western Canada, and we want to see the farmers of western Canada given assurances which will make it possible for them to carry on their plans for next year and for succeeding years with a much more definite knowledge of what they may expect in return than they have yet had from this government in the years that have passed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say that our amendment happens to coincide with the Conservative election policy of 1949. I wish the Conservatives would fight as vigorously for the farmers for this principle of giving them a fair deal through a system of parity prices as they demonstrated they could do for the manufacturing industries in a recent debate.
Canada has been, is and will be an agricultural economy, this in spite of rather than as a result of policies followed by the present Liberal government. I just wish to take a glance at the proportion of the national income that agriculture generally has received during the past few years. The dominion bureau of statistics figures for 1954 farm income show that the net farm income dropped to $1,125,600,000, or more than 30 per cent below the $1,669,600,000 net farm income for 1953. This follows up the significant trend that has developed in the last five years, when agricultural income has dropped most significantly from the peak level of 1951.

Agriculture
As the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort pointed out, it is only reasonable and fair to request that those employed in agriculture, those making their living out of the soil, should be granted sufficient remuneration for their labours to give them a reasonable share of the national income. In 1951, the top year to which I have referred, agriculture received 11 per cent of the national income. But at that same time 20-8 per cent of the population were engaged in agriculture. The 1954 figure indicates that there has been a slight decrease in the numbers employed in agriculture. It is down to 20 per cent of the population. But they have received only 9 per cent of the national income. There are many ramifications to the decline in agricultural income, ramifications that must be corrected in the very near future.
As you find 20 per cent of the population suffering a variable income which is below 50 per cent of the share they deserve, then by virtue of the fact that Canada is an agricultural economy you will find other segments of our population that will suffer as a result of the low income accorded to agriculture. I have heard many times-and I consider it very valid

the argument that if you have a healthy agriculture you have a healthy Canada.
We have spent a great deal of time this session in discussing unemployment. We have discussed unemployment in the agricultural implement industry. Why was it so important at this time? It was important because the government had failed to give consideration to the welfare of agriculture, and as a result of that the income declined, so that they were unable to purchase the products of industry. Another aspect that must be considered in the stabilizing of the economy is not only those who are employed in the manufacturing of articles which will be used in agriculture but the hundreds of thousands whose occupations derive from the servicing of this important industry; and I am certain that the Minister of Agriculture, for one, would agree with that statement.
In considering the welfare of agriculture, I do not want to limit it to the farmer in Saskatchewan; I do not want to limit it to any sectional area. When we are talking in terms of agriculture, we are talking in terms of farmers all over Canada. We are talking in terms of the smaller farmer in British Columbia, the maritimes, Ontario and Quebec. It is generally assumed that those farmers who operate on the prairies are considered as operating factory farms. I have heard that statement made in the House of Commons. Nothing could be further from the truth. They have to farm on a large scale in order to
give themselves a reasonable return. They have to farm from 640 to 1,000 acres, and in some cases 2,000 acres, to give themselves the same return that those working in industry or in other agricultural areas in Canada could be expected to deserve.
At the same time, we have had a very significant trend showing up in Canada in the last few years. It has resulted from the fact that the farmers of Canada have not received a high enough price for their products to allow them to practise good husbandry. It will be noticed that the yield of wheat in Saskatchewan has declined from 18-6 bushels to the acre in the period 1905 to 1914 to 17-9 bushels to the acre in 1952, a particularly favourable year. That relates the subject to a very important problem which was given consideration and turned down by the government earlier this session. We must give consideration to this problem of conservation as it affects the farmer.
I think we must give consideration to this problem of conservation as it affects the farmers, because we must conserve the products we have today if we are to be expected to feed the population of tomorrow. The population of the world has doubled in the last 100 years. It is expected that it will redouble in the next 50 or 60 years. Therefore the farmers of Canada must be granted a high enough price for their products to make up for the failure of the government to follow a conservation program.
The farmers in my area of Saskatchewan are forced to seed their fields to grain each year, even though they know that good husbandry practice might dictate that they should put them down to grass and rest them for a year or two. But they cannot afford to do that because for every acre they take out of productive cultivation they are losing their income. If, on the other hand, the prices of commodities they sell are to be sufficiently high to allow them to carry on this managerial practice which must be employed if we are going to meet the challenge of the world food production in the years to come, they must receive a higher price for their commodities.
I have seen many fields which have been ravaged by floods and wind storms and which now lie barren and deserted because the farmer could not afford to carry out the cultivation procedures which would preserve and restore that soil. That is one of the sound arguments for the necessity for and the desirability of establishing an agricultural prices program which will give the farmers sufficient income to take care of their depletion. In industry the manufacturer is given a good allowance for his depletion but the farmer is given none.

Agriculture
It is all very well for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to say that the Agricultural Prices Support Act is taking care of the farmers of Canada, but at the end of world war II, when the Agricultural Prices Support Act was passed, it was to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture and to secure a fair relationship between those in agriculture and those in other occupations. It was a very noble intent but it is the same as with so many other things introduced by the Liberal government; that is as far as it goes. Although there is a revolving fund of about $200 million for this noble purpose, since the inception of the act little more than $80 million has been used for that specific purpose.

What I am
getting at is this. It has cost the government only $80 million. That is a rather small contribution to make in order to achieve a stable agriculture in all of the sections of Canada. That is a rather dismal record indeed.
Unless careful consideration is given to this problem of giving a sufficient return to the farmers all across Canada so that they can live in dignity and comfort on their farm holdings, I believe we are going to do much to jeopardize the economy of Canada. When

we are talking in terms of a guaranteed annual wage for labour,-with which I would agree-I would certainly press for a guaranteed annual wage for farmers. They are suffering from the vagaries of the weather from year to year. They never know what they are going to receive. When they receive bountiful crops, when they appear to be doing fairly well,-when they are told by the Minister of Agriculture that they are better off than they have ever been before- and when they receive five crops in three years, what do we find? We find that the farmers in western Canada who are making their livelihood out of wheat and the butter producers in other areas of Canada are in a very precarious position indeed.
It was pointed out in the Manitoba Cooperator that through a survey carried on by the Manitoba department of agriculture it had been found that the average dairyman- and this, incidentally, is an investigation of the better dairy farms-obtained 79 cents an hour for his labour. When we think in terms of 79 cents an hour for the length of day that a farmer must put in, it still does not make a big sum to be distributed among the farmer, his wife and his hired help. We will find that consideration must be given to resolving this problem so that Canada, which is and has been, as I pointed out, an agricultural economy, will derive its strength from its agriculture.

I am here in this house today 24 hours later.

By way of introduction to what I will say after 2.30, I may say that I had the privilege of going to Britain, at the invitation of their government, to examine into the activities of the farmers whose activities they thought I should examine into; and I had the privilege of visiting with them seven or eight farms, about half of them in England and the other half in Scotland. We did that over a period

of 10 days. In many of the things I saw there are answers to some of the things that are being said here today.

Many of the countries that adopted the plan that has been suggested here today have departed from it. We followed the policy which we adopted then in opposition to policies suggested by the opposition, which was a policy of parity prices. Just before we adjourned for lunch, Mr. Speaker, I was asked whether it was the Canadian government or the British government which had requested me to go to Britain and spend the last 10 days there. I answered that it was the British government. I think I should say in further explanation, before going on to discuss the resolution, that some weeks ago the British department of agriculture inquired as to whether I, as Minister of Agriculture for Canada, would attend the royal show which was this year being held at Nottingham. I agreed to do so. They then suggested that I spend two or three weeks in Britain as the guest of the British government, for the purpose of being shown British agriculture in operation. I think hon. members will understand why that invitation was readily accepted.
I left here on July 2, and arrived there the next morning and have spent the last 10
Agriculture
days in Britain. As I stated just before lunch, I was on a 15,000-acre ranch in the highlands of Scotland yesterday, and the fact I am here today indicates that conditions throughout the world are quite different from what they were a few years ago. We can associate with one another and learn a great many things much more readily than we could in prior times. In addition to that it also indicates that the means by which food may be transported from where it is produced to people who require it in different parts of the world have changed considerably.
I may say that on each previous occasion I have gone to Britain I have gone there looking for something; either trying to sell them something or trying to buy something from them that would be helpful to us. On this occasion, I had nothing of that kind to worry about. The British government invited me, and they put official cars at my disposal when I arrived. They planned the whole program for the 10 days, so that I did not need to do anything more than be ready to get into the car at the right time, get out of it when it reported back to the hotel, and look at the things that were shown to me as I went about and summarize what we had learned. There are one or two things I found out that I had not realized before. One of them is that in Britain they have what we in Canada call a large farm. I had always understood, of course, that there were estates there that were owned by persons who carried them down from the feudal period to the present, and which were quite extensive. But I did not understand that there are many farmers who are operating farms on their own similar in size to our large farms.
One of the first farms I visited was a farm of 800 acres. The next one was a farm of
1.400	acres, and the next visit was two farms operated together by members of the same family, one of 700 acres and another of 400. I finally finished up yesterday at a 15,000-acre ranch, on which there were 4,000 sheep and 300 or 400 cattle, and the facilities that go along with running that kind of a herd.
In addition to finding out there is that type of farm there, I found out also that the farms are just as completely mechanized as our farms. As a matter of fact, I doubt very much if you could find a farm in Canada of
1.400	acres with 26 tractors on it, but I found one there. Not only did they have the tractors, but they had as complete a storage for grain as you will find in the best elevators in this country, and a whole drying system to dry the grain just as complete as we have associated with our elevator system.

Agriculture
Then, going to the areas where they were growing fruit, they had orchards with a sufficient number of trees in them to make me ask how many they had. They could not tell me how many they had. They started to estimate it, and when they got through estimating I concluded that I had better get the facts before reporting them in this house or anywhere else because the estimates that were given to me would indicate that they had about as many trees on one farm as we had in some provinces. Those are all facts which I think are important in these days because we are talking considerably about marketing our products in Britain, and marketing here and there throughout the world, adding suggestions that certain things ought to be done.
I only want to say that I thank the British government for having given me the opportunity of going there representing Canada, first to be at the royal show and see the products of their farms exhibited in the manner in which they are, and then later on to go over the country and see the farmers actually operating their farms. May I say, too, when I said there were 26 tractors on that one farm there were also 55 labourers. Here we believe that mechanization has relieved us from the responsibility of having hired help and feel it reduces our farm population, but they have a considerable amount of help on these farms, and that hired help is well paid and well housed. So, I want to thank the government, through this house, for having given me the opportunity of being there. I want to say to the house, too, that if I have an opportunity of discussing my estimates at a later date in the session-and I hope I will have but if there is as much talking done in the next few days as there has been in the last two weeks I will not be able to be here, and my assistant will see my estimates through the house-I will be quite pleased to go into the details of the visit; what I saw there and the effect I think it has upon our production here and our desire to be in the British market.
Now, the question before the house at the moment has to do with parity prices. The motion is a motion to go into supply, and of course as always an effort to prevent the house going into supply is looked upon as a motion of want of confidence. The suggestion contained in the motion is that the government should give consideration to the advisability of establishing a system of parity prices on agricultural products. This morning I was very much surprised when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) gave his reasons for supporting that resolution. His reasons were that the plank in the Conservative platform

drafted in 1948 justified parity prices. Well, I have read that section over quite often. We heard it read this morning; and I heard the explanation that the gentleman who was most responsible for the Conservative policy on agricultural matters was the last leader of the party, Mr. John Bracken. And, having read the resolution, and having heard it read this morning, and having known Mr. John Bracken for a long time, I am a little doubtful as to whether any of those who sat in that convention had any idea that they were putting through a resolution in favour of parity prices, as they are known to those who moved the resolution in this House of Commons this morning.
The understanding of those who moved parity prices, as I have heard it explained many times, is that someone should determine what the cost of producing farm products is and, allowing for a certain amount of profit after that cost has been estimated, set an actual price and announce it sufficiently far in advance so that the farmers can go ahead and produce, with the guarantee that they would obtain that price on all they would produce, let us say, during the next two or three years, or whatever the limit of time might be.
Now, I am quite certain that that kind of policy would not be put into effect by a Conservative government if they were in power in this country tomorrow. And I am quite certain, too, that the plank in the platform does not mean that. As a matter of fact the plank in the platform is nearly an exact description of what has been going on in this country ever since the beginning of the war, if not before that-an exact description of what has been going on, with just enough difference in it in order to make it possible to say that it is not the same thing. But, in effect, if any party were to attempt to put that platform into effect, as announced in 1948, it would be doing what we have been doing at least since the beginning of the war.
The first thing we did do after the war started was to call together a conference of farmers to find out what they thought of the situation, and to indicate to them what we thought with regard to it; and then, after having discussed the matter for a day or so, to arrive at certain conclusions as to what ought to be done. Then we met from year to year; and we still meet every December in order to go over the facts again, and recite them in December so that the farmers may know what they ought to do during the remainder of the year-knowing that in this country in the spring of the year we put in

our crops, and put our livestock on the grass. We have been doing that through the years.
As a result of what the farmers did to meet war demands there was a strong agitation to do something about giving security to the farmers, after the war was over. At the beginning of the war the federation of agriculture, which was the only farm organization right across Canada at that time- there were not any farmers' unions; there was the federation of agriculture organized right across Canada, in every province-and that federation of agriculture came to us and asked us for marketing legislation. We told then that, while the war is on it will be necessary for us to take control of marketing in order to provide the food that is required for the prosecution of the war, and in order to take care of agriculture in general across Canada. While war is on we have authority to control production and marketing, because our constitution provides that when war comes the War Measures Act can be passed, and we can take over all the authority from the provinces, and do the things that we think ought to be done for the proper prosecution of the war.
We did that. Among other things we entered into contracts with Great Britain and, to a lesser degree, with some other countries, as to what food we would provide each year. Then we told the farmers what we had agreed to provide and the return they would receive. For example, by guaranteeing quantity and price we boosted our production of hogs to where we could send 700 million pounds of bacon to Great Britain in one year, and boosted our production of eggs so that we could send 86 million dozen where we sent only one million the year before the war.
We induced the farmers to cut down on wheat production, because we could not sell the wheat. We induced them by paying $4 an acre to cut down the acreage, and to go into production of those things that were needed and could be turned into cash during the time of the war.
If anyone suggests that was not the policy, and that if so it had nothing to do with assuring reasonable cash returns to farmers in this country during the war, then I am going to say to him that those who take that position were not familiar with what was going on during the war.
We came to the end of the war, or we were approaching the end of the war. And Knowing the possible drop in sure markets in Europe, we brought legislation before the house providing for $200 million to a board- such a board as was described to us this 50433-383
Agriculture
morning as being the policy of the Conservative party-a board that was going to sit down and figure out what the relationship was between the prices the farmers were obtaining for their products, and the cost of producing those products, and then establish a floor price which would make it possible for the farmer to get his costs of production.
It was never intended that floor prices would provide him with much in the way of profit. It was intended that the floor prices should be made to work so that they would save the farmer from loss in adjusting his wartime production to peacetime conditions. Our reason for that was discussed at the time we did it. I remember being asked by the then leader of the opposition, "Well, how long do you think this period will last?" Someone suggested that we put four years in the act. I said that it took longer than that at the end of the first war-the figure I used was 18 or 20 years; and the interim between the period of the war and the period following the war probably was longer than that. We said something ought to be done in order to stabilize returns to the farmers following the second world war.
What was the reason for that? The reason was that following every war we have had -not only the last two wars, but the Napoleonic war-every war of any considerable size the world has ever experienced, we have had a drop in farm prices. And, following that, as has been suggested by an hon. member on the other side of the house, we have had a drop in employment throughout the country, and a drop in wages. We had times we have come to call depressions. And our main point in bringing down the measure was to see to it that condition was avoided following the war that we had just come through.
All I wish to say about that now is that, in spite of what was said this morning, that objective has been reached and maintained, right from 1944 until the present time. We did not use that act at all until about 1947, the reason being that agreements were entered into during the wa rwith Great Britain and others, and were still in existence, and we were able to sell our products at established prices under those agreements, down to about 1947. Then in 1947 we had to use this act that is on the statute books, and we have been continuing under it ever since. We had to bring it into effect. We threshed out this question of parity when we were drafting the act. I sat in a committee until three or four o'clock in the morning before we brought that legislation into the house

Agriculture
discussing the question ol whether or not we should make it parity or make it something else.
I must say that when we had that discussion there were members of the civil service, as well as members of the government, and there was no one on the committee who would favour using the term parity. They said that word "parity" had so many different meanings in different places and to different people that the proper thing to do was to state what we were going to do. That is stated in the clearest possible terms in the act as it is now drafted. It is stated that the board set up under that act must make a study of the facts and keep on studying the facts, studying the facts from day to day, and when we do establish support prices put on prices which meet the conditions which were existing at that time.
We have been carrying on in that way during the whole period of time from then down to now. Someone has been getting up from time to time saying that we ought to have parity prices as they have in the United States. It is true that the United States started off with the idea of parity being the basis from which to work. Very shortly afterwards they reduced it to 90 per cent parity, and shortly after they brought it down to 75 per cent of parity on certain products. Finally they took some products out altogether, for instance eggs. The reason they took out eggs was that under the policy of setting a parity price for eggs and trying to store them for a possible market they had to utilize even caves for the storing of eggs down in the United States in order to find room for all the eggs that were being produced under a policy of parity prices. In the long run that did not help the egg producer down in the United States. It has put him in the position where the price of eggs there today is not as good as ours, and the United States realizes that. They have been changing their ideas of parity from time to time.
Hon. members come into the house and say that we should go back and start where the United States started, that we should have 100 per cent parity; that we should start with that and base our prices in this country upon that. I am going to say to the house that the experience of countries which have tried it, including the United States, is that they will not go back to it under any circumstances. The farmers would not wish them to. They have had experience with this kind of thing with the result that they have developed other lines of activity having more in common with what we have been doing from the end of the war down to the present time.

I have discussed this question many times. I have discussed it at annual meetings of the farmers' union and at annual meetings of the federation, not later than January of this year. It was after this discussion that they drew up the plan which they submitted later to the government in connection with support prices. They do not call them parity prices in the sense in which those words are being used in this house. I have grave doubts whether even the farmers' union does that.
I am a member of the farmers' union and keep up my dues. Someone on the other side of the house said that a member of the federation is not required to pay dues. Whether or not they are, I belong to that organization because I am a member of the wheat pool. As a member of the wheat pool I am also a member of the federation. But I belong to the farmers' union because it is generally known as an educational farm organization. They go out in my province and in other provinces in general and start advocating things in the hope that they will turn out to be good. Quite often they do. Recently they have been looking into this matter of parity prices. Not only have they been looking into it, they have been putting something down on paper. During the lunch hour I took a hurried look at it and I may be wrong, but I could not find the word "parity" in it. I have written it in myself.

organization set up in every province of this country and associated with every part of the agricultural industry.
The suggestion was made this morning that these men do not pay dues to the federation in the sense that you pay dues to the farmers' union. That is true only in part. They do not pay to the federation as such, but a member of a dairy organization pays his dues to that organization; a member of the wheat pool pays in some way; members of livestock organizations pay dues to those organizations; then all these organizations are brought under what they call the agricultural federation, which includes the fruit growers and everyone in agriculture. These people are organized right across the country.
After discussions and talk they brought in recommendations. These recommendations say what was condemned here this morning. They ask that the basic formula for certain farm products for 1954 should be according to the modernized formula recommended by the C.F.A. national farm parity committee. They set it all out here. They made it plain first that what they are advocating is not an actual, nor is it an incentive price. What they advocate is some form of guaranteed price which will not prevent trading above that price nor will it be high enough to induce unreasonably high production.
They then set out in a table which I have in my hand the results of applying their modernized formula. They go on to say that it would not strengthen the position of the farmer to attempt 100 per cent of parity; that the most you should have is 85 per cent of parity and the least you should have is 65 per cent of parity. Then they set out tables indicating the result. They show that 100 per cent parity for No. 1 northern wheat Fort William would be $2.05; 90 per cent, $1.84; and 85 per cent, $1.74. They state that the government should not be asked to make it higher than $1.74, which is 85 per cent. Eighty per cent results in $1.64; 75 per cent, $1.54; 70 per cent, $1.43; 65 per cent, $1.33.
They say that the support price should not be less than $1.33 and it should not be higher than $1.74. Well, the support price is $1.40, and it has been that for some considerable time. subtopic: SUGGESTED POLICY FOR STABILIZATION OF INDUSTRY
speechtext: Were they gilt-edged?
