speechtext:
If they were not gilt-edged, they would not bring the price. The hog price has been up to $38.50 a hundred during that period of time. It has never been down to $23. What I said this morning was that we have been attempting to set a floor price which would not drive prices down as the prices of eggs were driven down in the United States. Although the price has been maintained above the floor in all that period, the government has not got into it when they got close to the price, as they did at Winnipeg. I was kept busy on the phone by people phoning me from Winnipeg that the price had gone below the floor and people phoning me from Regina and saying the same thing. When I checked, I found it had not gone below the floor price, but they were afraid it was going to. The price went up again. When my hon. friend says the government does nothing about these things, he

is absolutely wrong, and the whole record shows he is absolutely wrong. Everyone in the business will remember that they went on paying more than 23 cents right away, after being checked by our staff, in order to obtain the hogs.
With regard to creamery butter, the average price is 52-6 cents, and the top is 59-7 cents. We have had it at 58 cents ail the way through. Everybody knows the story in connection with that. If it were not for the opposition, we would not have very much trouble with it; but the opposition listens to every harebrained scheme that is put up if it opposes what we are doing. They get out and shout about it, get in the newspapers and they talk just as they were talking this morning about 38-cent eggs. Eggs averaged 56 cents a dozen throughout all the summer months last year. Eggs are now up around 60 cents a dozen here on the market according to this morning's paper and in Montreal. Yet we talk in this house about 38-cent eggs. Then at the first of the season some of the fellows who have eggs want to deliver them to the government at 38 cents. Last year we had two weeks when the eggs went below 38 cents and the government had to step in and tell those that had put them below 38 cents that we would not take a dozen of their eggs unless the price was maintained above the floor or at the floor, with the result that inside two weeks they were up and they have never been down to that price since.
I just cite that example in order to show that the government does not just go away and leave this thing. We operate under it all the way along and the floors are maintained. Whereas a price of 38 cents is talked about, one year the average was 42 cents, another the average price was 46 and in other years it has been comparable to that. But some people take in nest runs of eggs and get 15 cents a dozen for them and then the opposition spreads the story over the country. As a matter of fact, nest run eggs cannot be supported. Such eggs are not properly graded and therefore you cannot guarantee prices of them.
This table not only indicates that our board has been working in the same manner as any other board would work if they were put on the job. This table indicates that our guaranteed prices are identical with the prices that the federation says we ought to be guaranteeing at this particular time. The farmers fairly well understand that. All the talking that can be done here about farm problems by persons who do not produce eggs, who do not produce cattle, who do not produce hogs-who do not produce any of these things -is not going to change the mind of the
Agriculture
farmer as to the proper basis for support. He does not read it in the first place; and if he gets it, in spite of himself, over the radio, he will probably close it off before it is finished because he knows better. Costs that are recited here as being the cost of production are not really the actual costs of production at all. If they were, the farmer could not remain on his farm at all.
I agree with much of what has been said this morning to the effect that if you do not keep the farmer on the farm and if he is not producing the food that can be produced in this great agricultural country and is not shipping it out, you are going to have difficulties. I agree with all that. So-called parity is not the solution for his problems. But I should like to ask any hon. member from western Canada or from eastern Canada to go out to any road allowance in his constituency and check off the families that came there and homesteaded, whether it was 50 years ago, 100 years ago or 200 years ago. If he does so he will find that in the great majority of cases, in any district in this country, the farmers who came out in the first place are still there or their descendants are still there and they are operating those farms. Over in the area to which my grandfather came out from Scotland-and yesterday I was in the area that he came from- the farms are still owned by some descendant of the family. The same thing is true in western Canada. Time after time when I have been speaking on the platform in my own constituency I have asked them to name to me half a dozen men who had ever been put off their farms in the district in which I was speaking and I have not yet had anybody get up and do so. There are all kinds of suggestions made that, if you do not do this or do not do that, then we may take action against you and foreclose on you; but the number of cases where foreclosure has actually taken place is very small.
When I was there last week before I went away I said to the people: I am going to Nottingham to the royal show. Two different men out of the audience came up to me and said: My uncle was a judge in that show before he came out to this country. In other words, the people we have here are the same type of people. The people who formed the foundation of our settlements right across this country are the same type of people who are farming the farms that I have been visiting for the last 10 days. It is remarkable the extent to which we still follow the same practices as they have been following throughout the years that they and their ancestors have been on that land, and we are getting results similar to theirs.

Agriculture
But again there is one thing that is worth while repeating even in this house. In that section of the empire those men are producing about twice as much per acre as we produce. The reason is that very seldom do they have a spell of weather such as that which they had while I was there. I do not know whether or not I took some of the western dry weather with me, but it did not rain from the day I got oft the plane until the day I got on again. It rained in Glasgow last night. They said they had never before had such a long dry period as that. Because they have not had such a long dry period-they had 26 inches of rain in a year on one farm I was on and they had 90 inches on another and so on-the result is that they produce 60 bushels to the acre of wheat and there is comparable production of barley and oats. With that production they raise much more livestock and dairy products per acre than we raise. As a result of that, and the fact that their market is sitting right under their nose in great cities like London, Manchester and Liverpool, they are able to carry on there with a greater population employed to the acre than we are able to employ over here, because we must content ourselves with shipping our products long distances.
In spite of what is being said in this house with regard to wheat, there is not any better way of holding our surplus in connection with agriculture than by holding it in connection with a product like wheat because wheat will keep for a long time. If it can be sold at a price which is stable, it does not make much difference whether it is sold in this crop year or in the next crop year in so far as the surplus of it is concerned. But if the price cannot be stabilized, that procedure can be fatal.
I should like to suggest that the quickest way out of the system that we are following now would be for the government to agree with what the opposition has moved and to bring in parity prices. We might be dreaming of a great future for six months or maybe 12 months, but by the end of that time we would be finding ourselves drifting back into the old plan that we had for marketing products before we had the wheat board, before we had marketing acts in the provinces and before we had any of the systems that we have now; and instead of having parity, we would have a competitive price brought about by conditions that exist elsewhere in the world and brought about by conditions that exist here in connection with marketing as related to production.
I understand why farmers are most anxious to get their wheat into the elevators. They

must get it into the elevators in order to get some cash, and they are anxious to get their wheat in. But I have not yet run across a farmer who is so anxious to do that that he wants to get rid of the wheat board and market it in some other way. I know there are some, but that "some" do not talk to me apparently. Those who are in favour of it still keep saying to the government: Whatever you do, do those things which are going to maintain for us the marketing system which we have for wheat now, and establish a system in connection with other products which will get us the same results as we have had in connection with our wheat over the years since the war. We are attempting to do that. That is our plan and our policy.
I should like to ask this house not to vote for a resolution because the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) says it is the same as the plank in the Conservative platform. It is not. The program of parity prices as enunciated in this resolution is not that at all. Then I want you also to bear in mind the fact that Social Credit at one time thought that it was not very difficult to get $25 a person a month in order to make people happy, but they found it extremely difficult to do it when they got into office. Other people were convinced of that fact but they have not thought much about it since. But when the Leader of the Opposition comes along, as he did this morning, and deals with the supplying of wheat to Poland, may I say this. He can say what he likes about what he said the other day, but the impression I got from reading the two or three line report that appeared in the press in Britain is the impression I got from reading his remarks now. He talked in questionable terms this morning about the 85 per cent that is being guaranteed, but in doing so he is talking directly against what he said in the early stages of his speech when he spoke in favour of parity prices. There is only one way you can get parity and that is for the government to guarantee that they will take out of the treasury and put into the farmers' pockets an amount representing the difference between the price that the farmer gets and what the government figure parity ought to be. When they do that they are taking exactly the same chance as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) says they are taking in guaranteeing 85 per cent of a crop sold in association with the organization that is set up to bring about that kind of trade with a foreign country.
In one breath he is supporting parity as proposed and in the next breath he is condemning the only thing that would ever make parity possible, namely, a guarantee by the

government that we will take out of the treasury of Canada the difference between what we are asking people to pay for the product or what trade in the product results in their paying for it and what we have said is the parity price. Let me repeat that when you do that, and do it for two or three years in advance, the experience of every country that has done it is that you get so much of the product that, in spite of anything the government tries to do, if they do not fix the price that is being charged to the consumer they will not be there very long to do anything about it.
We have been here longer than any other government Canada has ever had and are still here, and one of the reasons for that is that the people of this country in general agree with the policy that has been put into effect to regulate and stabilize the prices of food products. The greater part of our food comes right off our farms and the efforts that have been made in order to stabilize those prices have been such that the people want to keep us here just as long as we follow that policy, and that does not mean accepting parity as proposed. Therefore I am going to ask the house to vote against the amendment, and I am going to suggest to those on the other side who come from the part of the country that I do that they had better be careful how they vote.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. gentleman has carried us over to Great Britain. He has given us an indication of the degree to which every part of the world has become so close to every other part of the world. He has told us of the progress made by Great Britain in the rehabilitation of her agriculture. All of this was intensely interesting but he failed to deal with the amendment in the form in which it is drawn, the form in which it is to be voted upon by the house. That amendment reads:
The government should give consideration to the advisability of establishing a system of parity prices for agricultural products.
Agriculture
I endeavoured to follow the minister through the jungle of jargon and the multiplicity of words he used, and I found it very difficult to understand exactly where he stood. He said the establishment of parity prices for farm products might bring a degree of prosperity for a few months but that ultimately they would bring about an uneconomic situation dangerous and detrimental to agriculture in this country. He said that to bring into effect parity prices was a dangerous course, and then he proceeded to point out that prices now are higher than parity. I found it difficult, therefore, to understand wherein the danger would lie in bringing into effect a system whereby the farmer would secure a lesser price than he is receiving now. However, the minister did not answer one question. Why did we lose the British market for agricultural products?

subtopic: SUGGESTED POLICY FOR STABILIZATION OF INDUSTRY
speechtext: Because of Jimmy Gardiner.

subtopic: SUGGESTED POLICY FOR STABILIZATION OF INDUSTRY
speechtext: I have answered that so often that I would simply ask the hon. member to read Hansard.

subtopic: SUGGESTED POLICY FOR STABILIZATION OF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
I did not interrupt my hon. friend. I sat here and suffered. While there has been a great technological change in British agriculture and while, as the minister said, its productivity is high, the fact remains that Canada has lost the British market for agricultural products. The fact is that no matter how advanced British agricultural production may be, she still requires to import some 60 per cent of her needs. What we in the opposition want to know is why has Canada lost that very excellent market which for so many years was the backbone of Canadian agricultural marketing abroad?
True enough, Britain has changed her agricultural economy. She has expanded it, but she is still in the market. The minister did not explain why it was that the Export Credits Insurance Corporation had not been advancing money to Britain in order to provide for markets there if that was possible. He told us of the reception given to him by the British government, and that is to be expected. He went over there with no purpose in mind other than to visit and enjoy the hospitality of the British people at the fair and elsewhere.

Mention was made by the Leader of the Opposition that the matter of parity prices is not something new in the policy of the Progressive Conservative party. That policy was first established directly and definitely by Hon. John Bracken in his Lethbridge speech in 1943.
Later on, as the Leader of the Opposition said this morning, it was officially incorporated in the policy of this party. Successive sessions of parliament have seen resolutions regarding parity prices brought before this house by the Progressive Conservative party. One was brought, I think, in the year 1949. Another, which I have before me, was moved on March 23, 1953. I then moved a similar amendment to the motion to go into supply, seconded by the then member for Souris, Mr. Ross. It is reported at page 3208 of Hansard for that date, and reads:
... in the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to provide floor prices for agricultural products at such levels as to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship.
Today the minister was able to answer the arguments that have been advanced as to the need for the establishment of parity prices, but in 1953 he did not know what parity prices were. At page 3218 of Hansard of the same date the minister said this:
The only objection I have to the word "parity" is that I seldom know what people mean when they use it.

The minister says he did not say that. I must say that was my interpretation of his words. As long as they have wheat, their concern today is what is going to be done about marketing it. When is Canada going to take a stand in keeping with the aggressive policy of the United States? When are trade policies going to be undertaken and inaugurated with vigour and forcefulness?
Mention has been made of the Polish deal. There have been other similar deals in the last couple of years. As I understand it, no one has any objection and no stand has been taken at any time so far as I know by anyone in this party or elsewhere, in opposition to the sale or disposal of surplus farm products anywhere in the world, as long as we are disposing of them for a return that is reasonably secure and certain. No one has taken any stand in opposition to the need for securing markets anywhere in the world. Indeed, I am one of those who believe one way in which to overcome the impenetrability of the iron curtain is to promote trade between nations behind the curtain and ourselves. The stand taken by this party is that trade is needed. We have pressed for that, and we shall continue to press for that.
Canada is losing her markets for wheat. She has fallen below the United States. She was ahead of the United States for years, not only in amount but in her share of the world market. She has fallen behind the other great wheat producers. One of the reasons for this is the fact that the United States, contrary to its responsibilities under GATT and within NATO, has been handing out free gifts for relief purposes, and entering into barter deals for foreign currency at cut prices. Those are the kind of things that undermine international trade stability; those are the kind of things this government has accepted with equanimity. Indeed, on the few occasions we have asked what the government

was doing in order to protest against the attitude of the United States the answer was in effect; "We wrote them some letters; we wrote to protest." When the question was asked in effect; "What reply did you receive", the answer given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce was to the effect that a reply was not expected.
The United States is having fire sales of its wheat in many places, to the detriment of world trade. The United States still has a support price. No one claims that 100 per cent parity is requested or desired under this resolution. The resolution simply says that consideration should be given to the advisability of establishing a system of parity prices for agricultural products. In the United States the support prices on dairy products now amount to 75 per cent, and on wheat the support price in 82-5 per cent for the current year, this being assured by the fact that United States farmers voted in favour of a reduction in their acreage beyond what would otherwise have been the case.
Certainly the western farmer, looking at the wheat situation, wonders why the Canadian government has failed to inaugurate a strong and effective sales policy. It is true that the Export Credits Insurance Corporation has made a couple of these guarantee deals recently. One was made with Brazil in connection with wheat for $16,750,000. Two were made with Yugoslavia, one in 1951 and the other in 1953. One has recently been made with Israel, upon the particulars of which I do not think parliament has yet been fully informed.
Recently I asked a number of questions to find out the extent to which the ultimate net price to be realized for the wheat in storage in this country is being eaten up by excessive storage charges. No one knows the amount of unsaleable wheat there is in storage. No one has ever been able to get the figures. For some reason the wheat board and the government-today they have been associated, for the first time in my experience in this house-have not told us how much of tnis unsaleable wheat is on hand. No one knows how much is being paid for storage.
I refer you, sir, to sessional paper No. 131-D, brought down on June 17, 1955. On that occasion, in response to this question, "How many bushels of wheat were in elevator and terminal storage in Canada as of the 30th July, 1954," I was told there were 361,271,000 bushels. The amount at the same time a year ago was approximately 337,600,000 bushels. The next question was:
What was the total amount paid for elevator and terminal storage for all wheat in storage between the 1st July, 1953 and the 30th July. 1954?

The answer was that there was no information. Mr. Speaker, that answer is an evasion, a deliberate evasion. For the government and the wheat board to say there is no information available as to how much was paid for storage last year is either incorrect or reveals a serious lack of accounting responsibility on the part of the wheat board and the government.
Further questions were asked as to terminal elevators or other storage facilities owned by the government and leased to private companies. Can anyone tell me what justification there is for the government and the wheat board to rent out terminal facilities owned by the government to a private company, and for that private company to store government wheat and make a profit on the return?
Another question asked was whether any of these terminal elevators or other crop storage facilities owned by the government were leased to private companies or agencies during each of the crop years 1952, 1953 and 1954, and the answer was yes, that there was one terminal elevator at Port Arthur, the Canadian government elevator. I cannot understand why an asset owned by the government of Canada should be rented to a private corporation in which government wheat will be stored at the expense of the farmers of Canada, thereby assuring to the elevator company a very considerable profit at the expense of the Canadian taxpayers. Further questions should be asked regarding this elevator situation. The elevator company to which I referred is McCabe Grain Company Limited.
How much of the stored wheat is unsaleable? No one knows the answer. What is being done to secure markets? No one knows. All we do know is that two or three deals have been made, one with Poland and two with Czechoslovakia. Then there was one recently with Israel, and one with Brazil in 1952 or 1953. Which member of the government will rise and let the Canadian farmer know what is being done? Certainly the experience of the last year and a half has been that, perceptibly, Canada's grain markets are being lost to the United States and other great agricultural producers.
The minister has not answered the question of markets by a multitude of words. It can be answered only by attention on the part of the government to a study of the question as it is asked. What is to be done?
The right hon. gentleman said in effect, "You had better be careful how you vote on this." Mr. Speaker, you know what will happen. If they follow precedent, hon. members from western Canada will rise and say

they are in favour of action, and will speak about parity prices. They will even say they are in favour of them, and then when the vote comes they will vote against them. We believed in it; we were all in favour of it, but it was a vote of non-confidence."
I would ask the leader of the government to announce that each member in the house may vote on this question as on a nonconfidence resolution. The right hon. gentleman said in effect, "You had better be careful how you vote on this." All I can say is that in the next few months those who vote against this amendment will be spending a great deal of time explaining what they meant by their vote, when they voice otherwise.

We note his comment that the world is changing, and that conditions are different today from what they were a few years ago.
The minister's talk to the House of Commons this afternoon in defence of his agricultural policy was marked particularly by his usual deviation from some of the realities facing the people on the farms, who are today confronted with problems in a changing world. As other hon. members have said, the one big problem facing farmers today, the factor that has wiped security away from under them, is the fact that increasing costs of production have placed them in a position where they must go further and further into debt if they wish to continue in production. If the minister will look over the farm debt figures for the last few years he will see that wherever the farmer has endeavoured to mechanize his farm to increase efficiency in production, he has been compelled to go into debt.
The farmer has no control over the cost of those things he has to purchase. On the fMr. Diefenbaker.l
other hand he must accept whatever prices are offered for the commodities he sells. He is caught in a squeeze where he must do his utmost to produce at the lowest possible price and in the greatest possible quantities with the facilities he has. The result is that he finds his position becoming increasingly difficult.
He has had some degree of success in the last few years, particularly in the prairie areas of Canada, because in the three years prior to last year he had enjoyed a series of bumper crops which had produced quantities equivalent to normal production in five years. Since that time, however, he has run into difficulty. The minister seems to slough that off as if the condition did not exist, but I would point out to him that it does exist, and that he knows it exists.
Listening to the minister today one would have thought the farmer was in a most prosperous condition, that the prices set on his commodities make him perfectly secure, and that the minister has all the farmers-I believe he described them as representative farmers-coming to his conference in December to help him decide what prices shall be set on farm products. speechtext:
If you have a parity price program in which the farmer's selling price bears a relationship to the cost of production he will then have security. Of course the country will have surpluses. By instituting a parity price program the farmer can provide surpluses which the world could use.
The minister said this afternoon we have advocated that Canada should follow the plan instituted by the United States some 15 or 20 years ago. If he will look over what we have advocated he will see that we have advocated that the government institute a parity program and gain from the experience of the United States to avoid some of the mistakes they have made. I maintain that agriculture has a greater function to perform in the life of Canada and of the world than it is performing at the present time.
All the farmers ask is that they be allowed to produce. I would like to know why there cannot be food surpluses without creating serious trouble. It is contended that with the situation which exists in the world today there can be no such thing as a food surplus. There are a billion people in the world who are hungry, who are suffering from malnutrition. This is indicated by reports of the FAO such as we had this morning. I had the privilege of discussing this with the director of the FAO, and his story is that the hungry people of the world are looking to Canada. They see that we have surpluses and they wonder why they cannot have some of those surpluses.
Agriculture
They want to know why the democracies with their vast surpluses cannot distribute them to the needy people of the world. They want to know why the production knowledge Canada has should not be given to the needy people of other lands. These are the people who are being won over to the totalitarian ideas of communism. They look at what the democracies can produce and wonder why that production is simply stored up. They wonder whether the democracies are going to try to win them over merely by the production of bombs and other nuclear weapons. Would not the democracies be more apt to win over these people if these surpluses were distributed to them?
All the Canadian farmer asks is that he be allowed to continue to produce. Any surpluses should be distributed to the needy people of the world, and they should be told how they can grow two spears of rice where they are now growing but one, how they can improve their irrigation systems and their general agricultural efficiency. They should be told how they can live better. That is the kind of contribution Canada can make to the world. The Canadian farmer should be allowed to go ahead and produce. To him there is no such thing as a surplus. Plan our program in such a way that these surpluses can be used to the best advantage in winning over to the side of democracy the billion people who are looking for leadership and who will one day make a choice.
I maintain that this is the great job for Canadian agriculture. This is the great vision of the Canadian farmer. Whether or not they get leadership from this government the farmers of Canada must have a larger share of the national income. They will then produce so long as the rains fall. As the minister said, during the terrible thirties when there were areas where no rain fell for five or six years, there was no production and of course the income fell. The minister says no people were put off their farms through foreclosures, but he knows that at one time 80 per cent of the farmers in one province were carrying a mortgage debt.

They can still do a good job. A greater percentage of the Canadian population should be in agriculture. Canada should be working to her greatest capacity to help the world and help win

these peoples for democracy. What a senseless state of affairs it is when a producer must suffer because there are surpluses which the world needs. I think man is about the only creature who could create such a senseless state of affairs.
We are asking for an up to date program of agricultural production which will assure security for those engaged in this industry. The Canadian farmer is looking to the Minister of Agriculture to provide that leadership. He is looking to this government largely because he can blame this government for his present costs of production. During the war, when he was back in production, the Canadian farmer took the prices that were offered because there were price controls during that period. But when the war was over the price controls were wiped out, and it was then that the farmers' costs of production increased and since that time the farmers' returns from their production have been declining.

speechtext: There was no control over the price of wheat during that time.

subtopic: SUGGESTED POLICY FOR STABILIZATION OF INDUSTRY
speechtext: That is what you are talking about.

speechtext:
We are asking that there should be a parity price. The wheat board system of selling certainly is a tremendous improvement over the old competitive system, and I do not think one farmer out of 5,000 would advocate a return to the old system. But when he looks at what it costs him to produce his wheat, when he knows the cost of production in the United States, where they have a parity program and where they are getting $2.25 per bushel for wheat as compared with the $1.60 or $1.80 which he is getting, he knows he is not getting his fair share. What he gets is a return from the sale of his produce in the markets of the world.
I imagine this government is doing the best job it can in selling that commodity in the markets of the world in competition with some tough countries. In the United States, where they have the Commodity Credit Corporation, they can sell the wheat at a low price and still give the farmer his $2.20 a bushel. The Canadian Department of Trade and Commerce, in endeavouring to sell this wheat, has a job on its hands and has the support of this house in doing that job. The farmer is not going to continue producing wheat and selling it at $1.70 for many years if his costs of production continue to rise.

I agree with the minister that selling butter at 58 cents puts stability into the dairy industry, but that is not going to continue for very long if the costs of production continue to rise. Twenty-three cents at Toronto may be a price floor for hogs at a certain cost of production; but if the cost of production continues to rise it will not pay the farmer to continue production.
We could be selling our commodities in the markets of the world and farmers could continue to produce. But the costs of production are the fault of the government, because when they took off the price controls they allowed the costs of those things the farmer himself purchases to rise, such as farm machinery, oil, fertilizer, sprays, repairs, the cost of living for everyone, the cost of labour, taxes.	All these are part of the
constantly increasing cost of living in Canada as a result of the government's policy of doing away with price controls. Unless the farmer's returns increase along with increasing cost of production, then he is facing bankruptcy. Nobody can stay in business when the costs of doing business are increasing and the returns are decreasing. That is why the farmer is in the position today where he is only getting 9 per cent of the national income, although 20 per cent of the people of Canada are engaged in agriculture.
For the reasons I have outlined we support this amendment, which calls upon the government to institute a real program of parity prices based from year to year on the actual costs of production. It is the only thing that can give security to agriculture, the only thing that can place agriculture in a position where it can do the job that agriculture ought to do and thus enable Canada to take its place in the world and help win the world for democracy.

As I said, I do not agree with some of the findings of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, but what I have read is fundamental. The minister's statistics and the statistics supplied by the bureau of statistics support the view that the Canadian agricultural economy is in a very critical condition. In bringing down his Agricultural Prices Support Act in 1944 the minister stated:

But since that time the farmers' position has grown worse each year. I am not finding fault with others in our economy who are able to bargain collectively. Recently in the United States the automobile workers have been able to win a point which will guarantee an annual wage. Next year the price of automobiles will go up. The dealers will have a greater commission. All the people along the line will carry the cost. In the province of Ontario a few weeks ago the medical doctors decided that costs have gone up and that they should pass on to the people who are sick the increased costs in connection with looking after the sick. While there are protests here and there the medical doctors, through their

organization, are able to pass on to the people in the community the increased costs which they decide are reasonable.
The Minister of Agriculture said that he could not find any reference to the fact that the interprovincial farm union council asked for parity prices. I might mention that in the brief they presented to the standing committee on agriculture on May 23 they asked for a national agricultural policy. They asked for:
Establishment of a new national agricultural policy that will guarantee farmers parity prices for grain and all other farm products sold on domestic markets, and equitable floor prices for all farm products sold on export markets.
But in their previous submission on January 19 they said that Canada needs a new national agricultural policy. They said:
Recorded statistics indicate that agriculture in Canada has been a depressed industry more often than not. Over most of the years a large percentage of the farming population has never been able to do much better than eke out a bare, poverty-stricken existence.
Unfortunately that is an accurate description of agriculture.
I listened to the hon. member for Acadia with interest this morning. I was surprised that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, while participating in a by-election in Alberta, took time to discuss some of our farm problems. As reported in the Edmonton Journal of June 17 the Secretary of State for External Affairs said this:
I've heard Social Crediters say we should reduce our stocks of wheat by accepting foreign currencies or even by giving them away.
This has an appeal when we see our wheat piling up whilst others starve, but in Ottawa we have an obligation to keep trade on solid ground. If we started bartering or giving away, we would disturb international markets and in the long run we would injure not only ourselves but also those we seek to help.
We should try to keep trade on a multilateral, economic basis and disregard emotional superficial solutions to our problems.
I was astonished to hear that trying to produce food for hungry people is a superficial or an emotional solution to a problem.
Mention was made of "The Story of FAO" by Gove Hambidge. As I read this book recently I was interested in some flattering references to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. As all hon. members know, he was chairman of the interim commission. Under the leadership of the distinguished gentleman this is what FAO set out to do, and these are the exact words:
Food production must be greatly expanded.
The necessary technical knowledge is available.
To produce more food is useless unless markets are created to absorb it by a widespread increase in consumer purchasing power.

Each nation is responsible for seeing that its own people have the food they need, but no nation can fully achieve this objective without the cooperation of others.
A permanent international organization with a wide range of technical functions and duties, concerned with food and agriculture, must be established as quickly as possible.
Then for two years the Secretary of State for External Affairs acted as chairman. At the Quebec conference, in winding up the business, he outlined the objectives which were really worth while in connection with the formation of this organization. But Canada really has played a rather insignificant role in connection with carrying out these fine ideals which we accepted some 10 years ago.
When we get around to the estimates of the Department of External Affairs we shall find that we have $323,000 as Canada's contribution to the work of FAO for this year. That works out at about 2 cents or something over 2 cents per person this year. That would not seem to me to be a great strain on our resources.
As soon as this motion is disposed of we shall be coming back to the estimates of the Department of National Defence. In connection with those estimates we have an interesting section dealing with mutual aid. As part of our international contribution toward national defence mutual aid we have $5-9 million for ammunition and bombs; $4-9 million for aircraft engines; $5-3 million for armament equipment; then for transfers to NATO countries we have some $9 million. Then there is another section for equipment. Under this section for mutual aid there is a total of $175 million.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that $175 million for the Minister of National Defence for mutual aid compared with some $300,000 for the Secretary of State for External Affairs for FAO to carry out projects that he considered 10 years ago were important do not seem a fair distribution of the resources of Canada. I do not know how it is that the Minister of National Defence has so much drag with the other members of the cabinet so he can get $170 million for his mutual aid program, whereas to the job of helping to feed 1,500 million people in the world only about 2 cents each year for every Canadian citizen is devoted.
The Minister of Agriculture referred some time ago to the question of how we could hope to increase Canadian production and consumption of food and also help to feed the hungry of the world. As found at page 4209 of Hansard of May 27, the minister said:
Members of the house throughout this session have been suggesting that the Department of Agriculture should increase production to take care of
Agriculture
an underfed world and at the same time maintain producers' returns at a high level. Attention must be and is being given to both suggestions, but I am sure it will be agreed that what is done in one direction will influence what can be done in the other.
The minister is saying that we cannot produce maximum quantities, give our farmers a fair share of the national income, and also feed the hungry people of the world. Twenty years ago anyone who suggested that we could do both things might have been thought to be irresponsible, but I must remind the house again that during the war years we found no problem in Canada in increasing our own consumption and production and giving our products away at a tremendous rate. When the war was over we found ourselves with a much more valuable investment in plant and equipment than we had when the war started. The Canadian people had a higher standard of living at the end of the war than they had at the beginning.
I submit again that if the tragedy of a third world war should occur the Canadian government, no matter which party was in office, would find, as was the case previously, that whatever is physically possible can be made financially possible.
I appeal to members in all sections of the house to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort. The Minister of Agriculture suggested it was a want of confidence motion. There have been similar motions. I had an amendment some years ago in connection with the milk subsidy which was carried by a majority. The main motion was then put and we went into supply. We did not have a general election. All that has to be done is for the leader of the house to tell members on the government side to use their own best judgment and decide whether they do not think it would be in the best interests of Canada to have a system of parity prices so that those who are producing food in all parts of Canada may have in return for the food they produce a fair share of the total wealth produced by all in Canada.

subtopic: SUGGESTED POLICY FOR STABILIZATION OF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment before the house is very important. As has been indicated by the mover, we do not regard the question of a parity price system as affecting agriculture only, although it does have immediate reference to that sector of our economy. As a matter of fact we regard the question of a fair share of the national income for agriculture as being one of importance to the whole Canadian economy.
Some time ago in a discussion on unemployment the leader of this group pointed out

Agriculture
that it was no coincidence that over the same period and almost in the same percentages as net returns to Canadian agriculture went down, unemployment figures in Canada climbed. The two are closely related, because it is well known that farmers as a group are the best customers Canada can have. They are not only customers in the ordinary sense of being domestic consumers of goods and services; they are also good customers because they require for purposes of production a great many things that people ordinarily do not buy. I refer to things such as farm implements, fuel, hardware, tools and so forth, used by farmers in large quantities for purposes of production and the purchase of which helps keep the economy going and maintain full employment.
The Minister of Agriculture made a rather resounding speech today on the general question of agriculture. We have learned to be a little cautious, as I think most of the farmers of Canada have, about accepting at face value the things the minister has to say about agriculture. It is well known that he can make a very good case out of very flimsy material. In spite of the many generalities he gave us today, he made no attempt whatever to face the problem and explain why net farm income in Canada has dropped so seriously since 1951, and that is something that should have been done.
According to the latest figures available net farm income in 1954 dropped from the previous year by about 33 per cent. To put the drop in dollars, whereas in 1953 net farm income was $1,699 million, by 1954 it had dropped to $1,125 million. Taking the whole period from 1951 to 1954 the drop was even more pronounced. In 1951 it was $2,154 million whereas by 1954, as I have said, it had dropped to $1,125 million. This is a drop of almost 50 per cent over that period of time.
When the net farm income of agriculture in Canada drops in three years to the extent of about 50 per cent, then certainly neither the Minister of Agriculture nor any member of the government can disregard the situation or explain it away in general terms by telling us that what the government is doing today is what they set out to do during the war, or anything of that kind. In addition, what is apparently not being taken into consideration by the Minister of Agriculture is the fact that at the same time the drastic drop of almost 50 per cent in net income occurred, which means a drop in the net purchasing power of the Canadian farmer, the cost of production actually rose instead of declining.
Not only that, but when we speak of parity we are asking, as our amendment indicates,

for what we think is simple justice, and in my opinion we are not being at all unreasonable. We are asking that as the result of an over-all price policy agriculture should receive its fair share of the national income. Obviously if the net income of agriculture has dropped by almost 50 per cent in three years, that in itself indicates that agriculture is not receiving its fair share of the national income, even if other things were equal. But other things are far from equal.
I have already pointed out that the cost of production has actually risen. In addition to that, we find that some of the industries in Canada, in fact the manufacturing industries of Canada as a group, according to the latest figures which I have here, dated July 11, have been experiencing a rapid increase in income. Dividend payments by Canadian companies in July reached a total of $54,572,373, as compared with July, 1954, when they were $47,109,721, a very substantial increase for the month of July. The cumulative total of dividend payments for the first seven months has now reached $347,507,388, and there are indications that by the end of this year it will reach record levels.
Those are the dividend payments. To them would have to be added the undivided profits, plus the amount placed in reserve, plus depreciation and depletion and all these other accumulations of wealth that go to make the total income of industry. During the same period when the manufacturing industries of Canada were increasing their dividend payments by as much as $7 million over last year, we find that agricultural income dropped by approximately 33 per cent.
This causes us some concern, and we look at this thing in a very serious manner. We are not out to ask for anything more than we think is due to agriculture in Canada, but we do intend to plead the case of Canada's best customer and biggest producer in relation to what has happened in our economy recently. Whereas the basic industry of Canada, which is still agriculture, has suffered great setbacks in the last three or four years we find that other industries are having a field day.
There is also some relationship between those two factors, Mr. Speaker. After all it could be that the one's gain is the other's loss. It may not be on all fours, but it certainly would indicate that if someone is losing his fair share of the national income while someone else is gaining it, then the person who is gaining it is doing so at the expense of the one who is losing it. That is the basic reason for this motion. We are asking the government to set up a price policy, which

we call a parity price system, in order to bring to agriculture its fair share of the national income.
In his reply today the Minister of Agriculture attempted to make a case, first of all, by proving that the government is now following a sort of parity price policy under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. Then he shifted his ground a little toward the end and stated quite categorically the government is not in favour of a parity price policy. He gave certain reasons for it, but I think it is indicative that for perhaps the last three years, at every farm organization convention and practically every local meeting at which I have been present, the question of parity prices has always come up.
The minister seems to find it difficult to locate a reference to parity prices in the resolution or submissions of the interprovincial farm union. I would suggest to him that if he were to read the resolutions passed at the most recent conventions in the three prairie provinces he would find abundant references to parity prices in very specific terms. There is no question but what both the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the interprovincial farm union are committed to the principle of a parity price system, though they may differ in some of the details as to how it should be applied.
There is no question, either, but that so far as the members of this group are concerned we are committed to the principle of parity prices for agriculture. We have no hesitation in saying that the government itself has a moral pledge, or shall we say a moral responsibility, for bringing about the stabilization of agricultural prices. I shall place on the record the words of the late prime minister himself, used in a broadcast in 1947 when speaking to agriculture specifically. He said:
If to help win the war, the farmers are asked to accept a ceiling on prices, we believe they are entitled to a floor under prices to insure them against an agricultural depression after the war. As an essential part of its post-war policy the government intends to ask parliament at the next session to place a floor under the prices of the main farm commodities.
The minister will say that pledge was carried out by passing the legislation referred to as the Agricultural Prices Support Act. Two of my colleagues have already referred to section 9, subsection 2 of the act which sets out as the objective of the board that the board shall endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture by promoting orderly adjustment from war to peace conditions, and shall endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.
Agriculture
The minister referred to that section also, and said it sets out in clear, specific terms just what is the policy of the government. A careful reading of that, if it means anything at all, would indicate it could mean only one thing, a parity of income for agriculture as compared with other occupational groups in Canada. Unless the government is today prepared to argue that they have achieved that parity and are maintaining it, then of course even on their own admission they are not living up to the policy which was set out in the Agricultural Prices Support Act and in the radio speech delivered by the late prime minister.
The figures I have already quoted I believe are evidence which cannot be contradicted that the government is not maintaining that pledge and is not carrying out its stated policy, if that is what it means by talking of parity of income for agriculture; because, as I have pointed out, agricultural income has dropped almost 50 per cent in the last three and a half years. Since the cost of production has actually gone up, the relationship is simply not there. As the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) and others have pointed out, percentagewise the agricultural population of Canada represents about 20 per cent of the people, but their income is somewhere between 9 and 10 per cent.
In view of this the government certainly cannot argue that they have achieved this fair relationship which they express in such euphemistic terms in the Agricultural Prices Support Act. That being so, I think it is necessary for this parliament to address itself to that question and try to evolve a policy which will bring a fair relationship between agricultural income and other occupational groups.
In my opinion there are two main ways in which that can be accomplished. Let me say at the outset that if either of the two ways I am going to mention is accepted it will mean a challenge to the present economic system, to some extent. It will require some interference with what is normally called the free enterprise system. Perhaps for that reason we will find that members on the government side, members of the official opposition, and perhaps even our Social Credit friends to the left will not find themselves able to go along with these two methods.
One of the methods by which parity as between agriculture and the rest of Canada can be achieved in what we normally describe as a high-priced economy, which I think would be comparable to the situation today, would be through a system of subsidies. In other words parliament would have to decide

Agriculture
that a certain price was required in order to bring to the farmer a fair price for his produce, in relation to all other prices in the nation, and be prepared to pay the subsidy out of the national treasury to the extent that that price at any time fell below the open market price at which a commodity could be sold.
Let me hasten to say this, because sometimes when one mentions subsidies and the national treasury in the same sentence people get visions of someone digging in for great handfuls of money to hand out in the form of subsidies. Let me say that to commit parliament to a policy of floor prices and a willingness to pay a subsidy when necessary does not necessarily mean any cost to the public treasury. It does mean that we are prepared to say to the world that in our own nation there will not be any fire sale of agricultural products, and that we consider agricultural production so vital to our economy and consider agriculture so important a section of the Canadian economy that as a nation we are prepared to stand behind a certain policy so we will not sacrifice that section of our economy on the altar of competition on the world market, or however it may be described.
To some extent the Minister of Agriculture argued the same thesis this afternoon, when he tried to impress us with the fact that even though under the Agricultural Prices Support Act there were certain times when none of that revolving fund was used in the form of support prices, yet the very fact that it was there and that the government was prepared to use it, and had authority to use it, had an influence on the market to the extent of keeping the price at or above the floor.
If what the minister argues is true-and I have no reason to doubt his word, because administering the act he is in a position to know-then certainly that can be extended. That same argument can be extended in relation to the whole agricultural policy in Canada.
I am quite prepared to admit that there may be situations and conditions and times where subsidies on some commodities required over a period of time would cost the public treasury a certain amount of money. If that happens, what are the objections? Those who oppose the idea of subsidies-and there are members in the house who quite sincerely, they say, hold that view and do not believe in subsidies on agricultural products-will have to remember that if we are going to follow that through we
[Mr. ZapUtny.l
will have to go back over a long period of Canadian history and reverse the trend that has been growing up.
So far as manufactured products are concerned, Canada has been committed to a system of subsidies for 60 years, or perhaps closer to 70 years. From the time the late Sir John A. Macdonald came out with what was known as the national policy, under which he persuaded the people of Canada that it was desirable to set up a tariff system to keep competitive goods off the Canadian market and, in that way, promote the development of a Canadian manufacturing industry, Canada has been committed to a huge and perhaps unending system of subsidies.
There is no greater subsidy, nor has there been any greater in the history of Canada, than is found in our tariff structure. I am not saying this in criticism of the position taken by members from manufacturing areas when they argue for protection. However, I do make these observations so they will realize what has been the effect of that kind of policy. If they will stop to realize what the consumers of Canada and particularly, as I have pointed out, the farmers, who buy perhaps a great deal more in proportion than do other people, are paying every year, every week and every day on manufactured articles by way of direct subsidies to Canadian manufacturers because of the fact that the protection is there, they will realize at once that this runs into hundreds of millions of dollars each year which comes out of the pockets of the consumers and goes into the hands of Canadian manufacturers so they may enjoy higher prices.
That is a subsidy; it cannot be called anything else. You may call it protection; you may call it customs duties; you may call it tariffs or any other name you wish, but it is nothing more or less than a direct subsidy taken from the pocket of the consumer. The only difference is that it does not channel its way through the public treasury; it goes direct from the pocket of the consumer to the income of the manufacturer. Then I need only mention the fact that we have been committed to a system of subsidies on the production of coal, gold and iron and steel, as well as subsidies on transportation on our railways. These have been going on for years.
The people in western Canada, particularly the farmers, are aware of these facts and are willing to play their part in the national economy. They say that perhaps some of these things are necessary. They are willing to go along with it in the interests of national

unity and the promotion of Canada as a nation. But when the shoe is put on the other foot; when a modest attempt is made to get some sort of guarantee from parliament in connection with agricultural products which, after all, are still the most important production in Canada, and when an effort is made to have some form of insurance through a system of subsidies, if necessary, immediately we are met with the argument that subsidies in themselves are evil, that in principle they are not good.
Without discussing the question of whether subsidies in themselves are good or bad, let us at least be fair in our discussion. If we are prepared to subsidize manufacturing industries in eastern Canada to the tune of hundreds of millions of dollars each year, so those moneys are taken directly from the pockets of the consumers and placed in the coffers of the manufacturers, then certainly as a parliament we should be prepared to pass legislation which would serve as insurance to the producer of farm commodities, so he will not be faced with a fire sale each time he has a surplus. That is one method.
The other method that could be employed would be in what we might describe as a low-priced economy. So far I have been talking about what is normally described as a high-priced economy. In a low-priced economy we could achieve the same objective through a system of price controls. As a matter of fact that was what the government indicated was its policy during the war years and the years immediately thereafter.
I can remember so well, as I am sure other hon. members do, that when the British wheat agreement was entered into in 1946, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Agriculture and the then prime minister made quite a case in the house for that agreement on the basis that, in the long run, it would be better for the agricultural industry in Canada to enjoy a stabilized market, even though it would not have the peaks of high prices, in order to avoid the deep valleys of low prices.
In other words their whole story at that time, their whole objective, was stabilization. They said, "We know the Canadian farmer will not be receiving as much for his grain under the British wheat agreement as he would on the open market at this particular time, but we also know that with such a system of commodity agreements, such a system of guaranteed prices, the farmer will have security which will enable him to plan his production and carry it on with confidence from year to year."
