I refer to the preparations for home defence. When this question has been discussed in previous years the reply has been that our 10 auxiliary squadrons were the backbone of home defence. From the remarks of the minister I take it that now that policy has been reversed, that the auxiliary squadrons are being withdrawn from defensive responsibilities and that the nine active force squadrons are going to be placed in the front line of our air defence.
The minister also indicated tonight that the whole matter of the future of the auxiliary squadrons is still under consideration. From that I take it that perhaps it has not been decided to withdraw them from fighter-interceptor activities. I wonder whether bolstering these auxiliary squadrons with a heavier percentage of permanent force personnel might not help get around the difficulty of coping with modern, complex military aircraft?
Along the same line, may I say that I cannot quite understand how it is that we are reducing our expenditures-and I raised

Supply-National Defence this point last night-for the procurement of aircraft by $100 million. I cannot reconcile that reduction with the need for the equipping of several of the active fighter squadrons with the CF-100 type of aircraft. The inference I draw from that answer is that we have a surplus number of CF-lOO's already produced and waiting to be manned by aircrew personnel; and that in turn would suggest that there must be a shortage of adequately trained personnel to man these aircraft. I wonder what the true situation is. Is there a shortage of trained personnel to man the aircraft, or is there overproduction in the CF-100 type of aircraft?

subtopic: SUGGESTED POLICY FOR STABILIZATION OF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
To deal first with the spending last year and this year in respect of aircraft purchased, I think last year our estimates contained an item of $395 million. This year, as the hon. member has said, it is about $100 million less, or $293 million. The fact is that last year we spent $309 million of the estimate, so the difference this year is $16 million.
May I say that there is also another phase of the matter which I overlooked in replying to the hon. member for York West. There are quite substantial savings in costs of airplanes as the production schedule runs along. In other words the manufacturing companies learn by experience how to cut their costs. So that consideration enters into this figure as well.
To refer again to the question of aircrew, may I say that we are not short of aircrew. We are getting aircrew to the extent on which we have planned. We had done so up until the end of last year, and I think the situation is still being maintained.

speechtext: In his reply, then, the minister suggests that there is no overproduction of CF-lOO's and that the present output of, I believe, seven aircraft a month will be sufficient to equip the remaining nine active force squadrons still not equipped with the CF-100?

However, I do not want to give the impression which seems to have been gathered by the hon. member who has just spoken, that the auxiliary squadrons are not now equipped with any aircraft; or that it has been decided

that the auxiliary squadrons will not be equipped with CF-lOO's. There is no decision yet, but we hope to have one in the reasonably near future. We are making very intensive studies for the reasons I gave earlier in the evening.

However, leaving that for the moment I should like to refer again to the return on recruiting for aircrew that was referred to last night. The minister qualified the original return by indicating that the third category, those turned down for other reasons, amounting to 3,729, included 1,207 people who merely made an inquiry and also 1,393 who made a contact and voluntarily withdrew before being examined and enrolled.
That brings us to a figure of some 2,500 who were approaching the net. They had actually made the initial contact or had made inquiry, and I imagine they would be supplied with all the necessary information regarding enlistment for aircrew training. Half of the 2,500 went further than initial inquiry and, as the minister expressed it, made a contact.
There is not much difference between an inquiry and a contact, but it seems to me the fact that 2,500 young Canadians were sufficiently interested to make an initial approach concerning recruitment for aircrew training and then backed away would suggest that perhaps there was something wrong with the initial counselling, if I may use that phrase, that is given to these young men.
It would also seem to me that perhaps the initial information given regarding the aircrew training program must have a discouraging effect to a certain extent. Last night I raised the question of risk pay. I wonder whether the minister would comment as to any possible deterrent effect that pay levels or such factors as risk pay might have in discouraging these 2,500 young men to whom I have referred. Has he any explanation why, after the initial contact, such a large number did not go further with their intention?

If there is any sign that a man will not make a successful pilot we think it is economical to dispense with his services as soon as that is realized. In the second place, those we keep in the service have to be of an extremely high standard.

I mentioned the question of aircrew a moment ago. We need about 900 new applicants to train each year. Last year we had 885, so we are fairly close to the mark.

I do not know how these things happen, but this is not the first time there has been an occurrence of this kind in Vancouver. Not so many years ago the government made a deal with certain people who were prominent Liberals under which a building was constructed called the Alvin building. It is now occupied by the unemployment insurance commission. This building was rented for some years; then a deal was made with the government under which the people who built it got an extremely high rent. Finally the government bought it. In my opinion, and I am sure this is the general opinion in Vancouver, the government lost several hundred thousand dollars in that deal.
Then we have the case of other prominent Liberal party people who rent buildings for postal stations and that sort of thing. I have raised this in the house at more than one session. I am really amazed that now, in 1955, we have another deal of the same kind. I think between the two ministers some explanation should be given of why it is that prominent Liberals are able to rent these buildings to the government at exorbitant rentals. It may be that there was a deal with these people that if they constructed the building the government would then rent it for a certain amount. What is really most important here is a question of the propriety of friends of the party in power doing business with the government in this way.

I did not get the significance of the question asked by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, nor did I get clearly the significance of the answer given. However, I am raising a question which I believe is pertinent to the discussion and which has to do with air force personnel recruited into that force for the five-year course. I am wondering how many of them receive permanent commissions. Would the minister tell us, with as much accuracy as possible, the number recruited each year for these purposes and the number who remain in the air force after the five years has expired?
I fancy there is a considerable number of young air force personnel who, after taking the course, find themselves without permanent commissions, and are let out by the air force at an age when it is difficult for them to readjust to civilian life. I have in mind an example, which I fancy is common, of a young man who joined the air force during the war at the age of perhaps 19 or 20. He may have had excellent service during the war and may have received a commission as pilot, as flight lieutenant or some other rank. After the war he was demobilized. Then perhaps after a couple of years he was urged to re-enlist and was given a commission on enlistment. After taking the five-year course he may have reached the age of 30 or 32, and if he does not meet the required standards he is let out. Young men of this kind have no other profession. Some of them may have enlisted from high school. They find themselves in civilian life with only the training they have received in the air force.
I am not making these remarks in any spirit of criticism, because I realize that if air force personnel are to be retained with officer ranking they have to be of a high
Supply-National Defence standard. However, it does seem to me that after having received a commission and gone through a course, even though a person may not have met the standard and had to be let out he should be able to remain in the air force and be of considerable service. I find it hard to understand how a young man could receive a commission during the war and then, after taking a course, be let out as being of no further use to the air force.
Surely there is something they could do. My plea is on behalf of these young men who are thrown into civilian life but with no civilian experience. Even though they are still comparatively young, perhaps 10 years or more of their lives have been spent in the air force. Surely some arrangement could be made to retain them. Would the minister enlighten the house on the point? If he does not have the figures he could take what I have said as notice and reply later. Perhaps he would tell us how many have been taken in for that purpose during the past number of years, and what percentage are retained after the five years have elapsed.

The permanent officers of the Royal Canadian Air Force, those who secure commissions on enrolment, are university graduates who have taken an officers' training course. In addition to those permanent officers we have what are known as short-service commission officers. Under this plan a man who is not necessarily a university graduate is accepted for a term of five years. It is a contract for five years, as he and as the air force know at the time, and there may seem to be some disadvantage if he fails to get a permanent commission within the term of his short-service commission. However, that is the contract.
While he is serving his short-service commission, each year he is assessed for a possible transfer to a permanent commission on a competitive basis. At the present time about 60 per cent of short-service commission officers are made permanent. In other words about 60 out of every 100 make the grade. As of February of this year we had on strength 3,322 short-service commission officers.

I should like to direct the attention of the minister to a matter which was first brought to his attention in a letter dated June 29, 1953. This has to do with a road into No. 6 repair depot at Dunnville, Ontario, which is a mile and nine-tenths


long. Because of the heavy truck traffic into the repair depot the township has been put to considerable expense for many years in keeping this road in repair.
This letter was written to the department by the clerk of the township on June 29, 1953, pointing out that over the preceding eight years the expense of maintaining this road had been some $16,000 and indicating that during 1954 it would be necessary for them to spend an estimated $6,200 to bring this road back to a reasonable condition. They were pleading with the government for a grant to help them under the circumstances.
This is merely a township road, and if it were not for No. 6 repair depot and this heavy truck traffic over the road the cost to the township of maintaining the road would not be great. The township did not hear anything from the department for a considerable length of time, although a representative of the department visited the officials of the township and offered them what I consider to be the paltry sum of $1,500 as a grant toward the upkeep of the road. This was in relation to an expenditure of well over $22,000. From that point until the present time the matter has been receiving the attention of the department.
I think I have been more than fair, due to the fact that I have not had an answer. No decision has been arrived at over a two-year period, and I think the department should be able to come up with some kind of an answer, either saying they are not going to give them anything or they are going to grant a reasonable amount for the upkeep of this road. The last letter I wrote to the minister was dated April 21 of this year. Previous to that I had written on January 18 and had a reply. As of today I have had no reply, though I have had several telephone conversations with the departmental officials. Surely it does not take this long to make a decision of this kind.
For sometime the story was going around Dunnville that this repair depot was going to be turned over to war assets and disposed of, but later we found out that was not true. We understand from correspondence that it is not going to be turned over to war assets but will be maintained by the air force. If that is the case surely it should not require this length of time to arrive at a decision on this matter.

The matter I wish to discuss, Mr. Chairman, is the matter which I raised on the 17th of June. It has to do with morale in our forces. I raised several matters on that date and indicated that I did not feel that a sufficient amount of care was taken as to the kind of people we brought into contact with our boys in the forces.
I think we have to be extremely careful about this matter in times as dangerous as these. I should like to read the remarks of Mr. Claxton, the minister who preceded the present minister, as they appear in the introduction to volume I, No. 3, the 15th November, 1951, issue of Current Affairs. It is to be borne in mind that this periodical, Current Affairs, comes out twice a month, if I am informed correctly, and goes to all men and women in our services. The result is that whatever is in these pamphlets very likely has a considerable influence on the boys and girls in the forces. Here are the words of Mr. Claxton:
Men and women serve best when they serve from conviction-
May I mark the word "conviction".
-when they know what they stand for and believe in what they know. Particularly they should know as much as possible about Canada and the countries and peoples joined with us in the great effort to prevent a large-scale war.
Further down I read:
The bureau of Current Affairs will carry out its work by the production of pamphlets dealing with current affairs of national and international concern, Canadian citizenship and topics of a general nature.
Further down I quote the closing paragraph:
It is a primary responsibility of commanding officers to make every possible use of this information program and to make available all the facilities required to ensure its success. Its success can be a real factor in the efficiency of our armed services.
Those are important words. They have an important meaning. One can see the amount of responsibility they place on the officers in the forces. Consequently if a copy of Current Affairs such as some of these that I think we shall bring to the attention of the committee goes into a unit and the officers do their duty as it is placed upon them by these words, then there will be a definite undesirable influence created on the boys and girls who are under their charge.

I should like to draw to the attention of the committee that we are in a cold war and surely this does not need to be repeated- and that a cold war is a war for men's minds. The side in this struggle that is going to win is the side that is going to win the other people's minds. Let us bear that fact in mind. The enemies we are fighting do not particularly care whether they attain their objective this year, five years from now, 10 years from now or 20 years from now, so long as they attain it. They have been working on this thing for hundreds of years now, and a few more years will not make any difference so long as they can keep on winning. I do not think there is anyone in this chamber who will express doubt that they are winning. They have been winning for 20 years and we are just sitting ducks for them to practise on.
Some of the things that have been done to the thinking of the Canadian people and the United States people strike me with absolute horror and amazement. I would not have believed that such an effect could have been produced on our people as that which has been produced by the clever devices used in this cold war.
So we are being attacked with the weapons of a cold war, a war for men's minds. Our enemies are seeking to establish in the minds of our people certain false conceptions, impressions and attitudes. Each of these conceptions, impressions and attitudes is a weapon against us. If it finds its mark, it produces its effect; and they are finding their mark. Most of us do not seem to act as though we realized that.
Yesterday or the day before yesterday we had an example here that amazed me, when the Leader of the Opposition rose and raised the matter of headlines which appeared- and which were carefully designed, I would imagine, two or three years ago

concerning the terrible danger of atomic bombs and the like, and people were called on either to avoid war or be exterminated. The matter was raised here and you would have thought the house had been struck by a tornado from the effect that was produced.
Then up to his feet got the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and continued the general impression. The house just looked almost stupefied because of the effect of that clever move on the part of our enemies. It was designed just to produce a softening effect on us; to make us ready to give up almost anything rather than get into a war; to make us go to the big conference and be all ready to say to them, "Now, what do you want? Just tell us and we will pass it over to you".

That is just about the attitude that was manifested by a great number of members in the house, as far as I could judge, and by a great many people across the country. Mr. Chairman, we cannot go on having these things happen for too long without being destroyed. That gives the general idea I wish to develop. Anyone writing or speaking in such a manner as will lead to establishing any of these conceptions, impressions or attitudes, through weakening us and strengthening our enemies, is following the communist line.
There is a good deal of question as to what constitutes the communist line. May I say that the communist line is anything that is getting people into the idea that they will give the communists what the communists want. That is the communist line. If it appears in a newspaper editorial it is a communist newspaper editorial, in effect, no matter what kind of man writes it or what paper contains it; and if it appears in one of these books it is the communist line just the same.
What are some of the things that communists want to establish in our minds, and certainly in the more or less tender minds of our servicemen? Here are a few of them. They wish to establish that the bolshevik ascendancy in Russia was a revolution. It was not a revolution; it was a conquest. The men who in 1917 went into Russia and beat down the Russian government came from the United States and Switzerland in armoured trains, after they got to Germany. Those who do not know that just do not know anything at all of what they are talking about in respect of Russian communism. The objective of these people is to establish in our minds that it was a widespread revolution in Russia that produced the bolshevik regime in Russia.
That is not true. If we have going into the hands of our youth a document in which that idea is inculcated or, to use a common expression, is "put over", then that document is not a desirable document to go into the hands of our armed services. I am preparing the groundwork so we can judge some of these Current Affairs pamphlets that have been going into the hands of our boys and girls.
The second thing communists wish to establish is that the bolsheviks were genuine Russians. They were not Russians. The men who established the communist conspiracy in Russia were not Russians. They were aliens, and they came from outside Russia, one body of them from New York city and one from Switzerland. Those who are well informed

If people think it is a way of life they will say, "The time will come when these people, these Russians and Chinese, will have enough territory and they will be satisfied. Let us give in to them just a little bit more". But if they know that the people who established themselves in Russia were a body of alien men, both in Russia and in the United States, they will know that these people will never stop until they bring the whole world under their feet. Consequently to establish in the minds of our boys and girls the idea that they are Russians that are in charge of Russia and China is to put them in a wrong frame of mind altogether and to weaken their morale, to cause them to come home and produce false impressions at home, and cause them to write home and do that.
Another idea they wish to establish is that Chinese communism was a Chinese revolution. Nothing could be further from the fact. I established that in my speeches in this house on April 21 and May 5, beyond peradventure of a doubt. It was not a Chinese revolution. It was a Russian conquest of China. The men in charge of China today are the agents of Russia and were put there by Russian force and Russian armaments and assistance. Anyone who indicates in any one of these pamphlets anything to the contrary probably does not know any better; but to entrust men like that with the responsibility and the privilege of writing one of these pamphlets is certainly a dereliction of duty on the part of those in charge.
Another thing they wish to establish is that communism liberates people. They are always talking about how they liberated this country, that country and the other one. They talk about how they liberated China, and all the rest of them. You have never seen a country on the face of this earth that was liberated by communism. They have been enslaved, every single one of them. They might have established governments, but they are under the ultimate domination of Russia. Even China is. There is another communist line.
Here is another one, that communist states need friendly neighbours for protection. Maybe they do, but what about ourselves? Do we not need some friendly neighbours? Does Britain not need some friendly neighbours?

Has not the glorious record of Britain over the last 1,500 years justified her in having friendly neighbours? Why should an arrogant Mongolian outfit in Russia undertake to tell Britain she has to have on her borders states that are friendly to Russia until Russia gets us completely surrounded, until she can destroy us? That is the situation. That is exactly what they are trying to do now. This big four conference at the summit is designed to soften us up and get one or two more friendly neighbours for Russia. The arrangement with Austria was with the object of getting a friendly nation. Surely all of it has been to get friendly nations, Czechoslovakia, Poland, and all the rest.
That is another communist line. Every other nation needs friendly nations and neighbours too. Who thought up the idea that it is the communists especially who need friendly neighbours, that the poor dear Chinese cannot be safe unless they have a friendly Formosa alongside them; and then Indo-China, Malaya, the Philippines, Japan, until they finally get to Vancouver and establish a hold on the mainland in order to have friendly neighbours? That is an astonishing thing. You would not think that would be imposed on anybody who was not asleep, but it is imposed on our people. Anyone who conveys that idea in an article is following the communist line.
Another communist line is that red China ought to be recognized. We are not going to enter into a discussion of the matter, but in my judgment the reds in China have never done a thing under the sun to justify being recognized except being ugly, monstrous conquerors in the crudest possible way, dispossessing people of their freedom. They have enslaved 450 million people in China and subjected them to the most outrageous tyranny they have ever had.

And they are just exactly the opposite to the Anglo-Saxon-Celtic nations. If there is anything they want to destroy from the face of the earth it is the Anglo-Saxon-Celtic peoples, above all other peoples.
It is a struggle between peoples believing in private enterprise and freedom, and peoples believing in public or socially-owned enterprise. It is a struggle between the British commonwealth and empire and their friends, as I say, and the rest of the world.
6104	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence I think every member in the house will agree with me that 40 years ago, before we had been vitiated by all this propaganda, the British commonwealth and empire was in our minds the greatest guarantor of freedom and peace and security on earth; and it is today. Whether we recognize it or not, it is today. Do you think you will find that in these documents? No, not a word.
The British crown is divinely ordained. The British coat of arms has divine biblical significance. What is the meaning of the lion and the unicorn? Are they just there by accident? It does have real spiritual significance. What is the meaning of the red in the flag? It indicates the covenant people. Who are the covenant people? There will be plenty who do not know, and I suggest to them it would be most entertaining for them to find out. But whether or not we are the covenant people, the British flag has deep spiritual significance. It consists of three Christian crosses, the three Christian crosses that go forth to struggle against the hammer and the sickle. It does not take long to tell on which side Christianity is, does it; or spirituality, or all the priceless things that make men great, and have made them great in the past.
The Bible is true. Many do not believe the Bible is true. The number who disbelieve the Bible is increasing, I am afraid. Nevertheless the Bible is true. Do you think you will find any evidence in any of these pamphlets that the Bible is true? No, not a word. Evolution as the result of mere blind chance is utterly preposterous. Do you think you will find any indication in these to show that, although the world is full of evidence which fairly screams against the very thought of evolution being the origin of man.
Now, the wonders of British history. Do you find any reference here to the remarkable deliveries that have been made for us, as in the case of the Spanish armada, Dunkirk, the time the breeze turned back the poison gas the Germans liberated against our men in 1917; the battle of El Alamein, when Providence just fairly thrust forth a saving hand.

speechtext:
I believe it is my duty at this time to say that it is the responsibility of the Chair to try to so administer the rules of the house that it will be possible to do the business of parliament within a reasonable time of, say, seven or eight months. I am afraid if the Chair continues to permit hon. members to get as far afield from the details of the estimates as has been done this evening we will not get through the business of this parliament within a reasonable time.
I say to the hon. member who has just taken his seat that I ask him, and others, to bear in mind that there are places in the parliamentary year where general speeches based upon matters of principle are fully in order. One occasion would be the debate in reply to the speech from the throne, and often there are other occasions when the departmental administration item is called in a particular department.
However, when we are dealing with the details of the estimates it is not in order to discuss a matter of that kind. The question before the house at the moment is whether or not a certain sum of money should be voted for certain purposes during the ensuing year. To the best of my ability, for the rest of this session I intend to be more efficient in holding the committee to a discussion of the item before it than perhaps I have been in the last few days.

subtopic: SUGGESTED POLICY FOR STABILIZATION OF INDUSTRY
speechtext: May I be permitted to say just a word. I want to assure my hon. friend and members of this committee that I am just as concerned in connection with the publication Current Affairs as anyone else. I would not be a party to the promotion of communism in this publication.

subtopic: SUGGESTED POLICY FOR STABILIZATION OF INDUSTRY

SUGGESTED POLICY FOR STABILIZATION OF INDUSTRY

We are now discussing the Royal Canadian Air Force, and I am afraid I cannot rule otherwise than that a discussion of official publications dealing with or distributed to the air force would be in order under any of the three services provided the same publication goes to the three services. I do think we have heard one speech which was not as pertinent to the publications going to the troops as it should have been, by and large; but it was my fault for permitting it to continue.
I do think the discussion should remain strictly pertinent; but if it is material having to do with the Department of National Defence I would not think it was out of order. I do not think I should be called upon to express an opinion as to whether on a discussion of the 1955-56 estimates, references to publications of 1951 or 1952 are pertinent. I think some effort at least should be made to show that the same type of publication is still being published.
